Pakistan rejoices as country’s first astronaut enters orbit

Zeeshan Ali makes history as the first foreign national to board China’s space station

The first person from Pakistan to go into orbit has made history as the first foreign astronaut to board China’s Tiangong space station.

Muhammad Zeeshan Ali docked at the space station in the early hours of Wednesday after taking off from China’s Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China on board a Chinese-made rocket.

Ali, 40, will stay in space for five to 10 days, shorter than the usual six-month stints Chinese astronauts serve.

“I’m not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder,” Ali told reporters on Tuesday.

While most of the infrastructure behind Ali’s space trip is Chinese, he has trained for months in China, including by learning Chinese, to make the trip happen.

“This is not just one astronaut’s journey, but the journey of 240 million Pakistanis. It is the journey of our younger generation, our scientists and our dreams,” Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said in a post on X.

“This is living proof of the ironclad friendship between Pakistan and China. We are grateful to our brother country, China, for making Pakistan part of this historic mission.”

Chinese President Xi Jinping said the joint mission with astronauts from China and Pakistan is “a vivid embodiment of the deep-rooted friendship between the two countries”.

This is a big diplomatic moment for China. Beijing is eager to show the world that the Tiangong space station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.

China has been ramping up its space industry and aims to put a Chinese astronaut on the moon by 2030. The US aims to do the same in 2028, for the first time since the 1972 Apollo 17 flight.

China plans to establish a ‌research ‌base on the moon by 2035 with Russia.

Both Beijing and Washington insist their presence in space is entirely peaceful, but the US has warned that China could seek to dominate resource-rich areas of the moon.

Bangladesh garment workers win 36% pay rise after weeks of protest

The protests have cost Bangladesh hundreds of millions, but it is unclear whether workers will accept the offer.

Workers in Bangladesh’s garment sector have been offered a 36 percent pay rise after months of protests that are estimated to have cost the country’s economy hundreds of millions of dollars.

The chairman of Bangladesh’s government-appointed garment industry wage board said on Wednesday that the “majority” of the board had agreed to increase the sector’s minimum wage from 12,500 taka ($100) to 17,500 taka ($136) monthly.

Bangladesh’s central bank calls the garment sector the “country’s export engine”. It earns roughly $38bn a year, employs four million people, and accounts for four-fifths of the country’s exports. Many of the industry’s workers are women in rural areas.

The 17,500 taka offered is below the 30,000 taka ($240) that protesters had asked for, and it’s not currently clear whether they will accept the amount offered.

“Although we are not completely satisfied, the outcome is not entirely bad either,” Babul Akhter, the labour representative on a wage board set up to resolve the crisis, told reporters. Akhter urged workers to return to their factories.

“Previously, workers used to get a wage revision every five years, but this time they are getting a revised wage after three years.”

The wage hike will take effect in December, with workers receiving the new salaries in January.

An economic success

The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) said on Sunday that protests had cost the industry an estimated $428m in losses, while orders worth $254m had moved to other countries.

Bangladesh is the world’s second-largest garment exporter, behind China. Home to 170 million people, the garment industry has proved an economic success story that has driven development in the South Asian country.

That has, at times, come at a cost: in 2013, the Rana Plaza factory collapse killed 1,134 people and injured thousands, exposing poor safety standards and working conditions for the millions of workers in the industry.

Numerous other incidents, including fires, have resulted in deaths – sometimes killing dozens.

Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco

More than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final, Senegal is Africa's soccer champion once again.

Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned an earlier ruling which handed the trophy to Morocco.

Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.

CAS has now rejected that earlier ruling, based on referee Jean-Jacques Ndala's decision to let the game resume after the protest.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport has delivered justice to sport," Senegalese soccer federation president Abdoulaye Fall said in a statement.

The legal battle may not be over yet after Morocco announced plans to appeal, likely to Switzerland's supreme court, in a challenge to the integrity of a senior CAS judge.

Tournament regulations said a team which refuses to play should be considered to have lost the game, but CAS said those rules were meant only for cases "when a team's conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently."

Ndala "did not err in law" when he resumed the game and had "sole authority" to make that call, CAS said, adding its three judges were unanimous.

"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," CAS said. "However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary.' On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."

Morocco raises concerns over CAS process

Morocco's soccer federation detailed plans for an appeal that targets one of the three judges on the CAS panel.

In a statement, the Moroccan federation protested what it described as the court's failure to address potential integrity concerns, alleging "confirmed communication" between German arbitrator Ulrich Haas and Fall, the Senegalese soccer president, 48 hours before the decision was issued.

The CAS director general, Matthieu Reeb, acknowledged to reporters at the court in Lausanne that a Moroccan protest was received just minutes before the verdict was announced.

Reeb said the court's panel "in charge of petitions for challenge has conceded that there was not enough elements at this stage to postpone the notification of the award."

CAS verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland's supreme court, also in Lausanne, though only on limited procedural grounds of which a judge's integrity could be one.

Haas has been among the most respected and in-demand CAS judges in the past 20 years, selected by parties in storied cases involving Manchester City's beating a Champions League ban by UEFA, tennis star Simona Halep's doping case and Africa's Champions League final in 2019.

Patrick Kabou, a lawyer for the Senegalese Soccer Federation, called the alleged communication between Fall and Haas "unreal."

Trouble on the field and in the stands

Senegal won the final 1-0 after extra time with chaos on the field and violent clashes in the stands. Even the ball boys were involved in scuffles as they tried to snatch towels that Senegal goalkeeper Edouard Mendy was using to keep his gloves dry.

The result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

Senegal beat AFCON host nation Morocco after a 15-minute delay in play. At 0-0, Senegal's team walked off the field to protest Morocco being awarded a penalty kick in the last minute of regulation time.

Match referee Ndala of Congo eventually allowed the game to restart, Morocco's penalty by Real Madrid forward Brahim Diaz — a slow chip shot known as a "Panenka" — was saved, and Senegal won in extra time.

The drama continued through the months of legal tussles. Senegal's players paraded with the trophy ahead of a game in March against Peru, even though Morocco was recognized as the champion at that point.

Both teams played at the World Cup believing themselves to be the rightful champion of Africa.

Soccer's laws versus regulations

Senegal had the laws of the game on its side, and Morocco had the tournament regulations.

The laws of soccer state that referee decisions are final. CAS backed that position with its own "field of play" doctrine, that on-field calls by a referee generally can't be taken to the sports court.

"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met — both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume," CAS said.

In the first legal case in March, CAF appeal judges cited AFCON tournament regulations that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorization of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition."

The CAS judges heard evidence at a one-day hearing last month and the court promised a verdict by the end of November with a full written ruling of its judges setting out reasons for their decision.

The next men's AFCON starts in June co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. Morocco will aim to end a wait for the title which now stands at 50 years.

Soccer fans in Senegal celebrate a win

"Senegal won on the pitch, and the court simply confirmed what we all already knew: We are the real champions of Africa," said Mariama Sidibé, 35, an accountant in the capital, Dakar.

Sidibé said the dispute between Morocco and Senegal should now be left in the past.

"With all of this behind us, we should focus on what unites us now, and who knows, maybe Morocco can have its revenge on the field during the next AFCON this summer," she said.…

Domestic violence soars to record high in Germany

Every three days in Germany, a man kills his wife or ex-partner. Every 10 minutes, the police record a sexual offense against a woman. "A shocking finding," according to Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig.

The German government has presented some grim statistics with regard to misogyny, rape, violence and murder, with reported cases of domestic violence at an all-time high.

At a press conference in Berlin on Tuesday, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, Family Affairs Minister Karin Prien and Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig released the latest figures on crimes that specifically target women: whether within families and intimate relationships, in public or online.

'Behind all these terrible numbers lie individual stories'

In contrast to the statistics pertaining to crime overall, which have remained the same or increased only slightly, reports of crimes against women have increased.

"Behind all these terrible numbers lie individual stories, people and particularly women and girls, whose lives are severely affected by these acts of violence," said Dobrindt.

In 2025, some 280,000 people were victims of physical abuse in their own homes, a 2.8% increase compared to the previous year. Over 70% of the victims were female. Each hour, 16 women are subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors.

The male victims included boys who had been assaulted by their fathers.

The number of misogynistic hate crimes has also risen dramatically, by almost 50%, to 819 cases.

"The figures show us what it can mean to be a woman in Germany," said Hubig. "It can mean being killed by one's partner or ex-partner. Being a woman can also mean being physically abused by one's partner or ex-partner in one's own home. Being a woman can mean that one's sexual autonomy is brutally disregarded."

Perpetrators, victims getting younger

According to the latest findings, both perpetrators and victims are getting younger. In 2025, nearly half of all female victims of sexual offenses were under the age of 18. And the number of incidents of online violence against women and girls rose by 15.7%. This includes the unauthorized sharing of videos and photos, verbal abuse, manipulation of images, threats and online blackmail, as well as cyberstalking.

Because many perpetrators and victims are still in their teens, Prien, who is also minister for education, said the government wanted to focus primarily on schools, which she explained should become places of prevention.

"Ultimately, we need to bring about a change in people's mindsets, especially those of men. That will be the deciding factor in the end," she said.

Femicides to be classified as murder, not manslaughter

Over the weekend, Justice Minister Hubig had already announced that in future all femicides, the intentional killing of girls and women because of their gender, would be classified as murders. Currently, such crimes are often classified as manslaughter, for which the penalty is less severe than for murder.

Hubig told German broadcaster ZDF that it was increasingly common that femicides be described as family tragedies or as domestic dramas revolving around jealousy and then classified as manslaughter.

Martina Link, the vice president of the Federal Criminal Police Office, was also at the press conference in Berlin. She called for everybody to pay closer attention to the issue, within their own families, neighborhoods or at work.

"Violence against women is not a private matter," she said. "Not in our immediate surroundings nor in the digital world."

She also pointed out that when it came to sexual offenses and domestic violence, only about 5-10% of cases were reported.

Big Tech could find it increasingly tough to secure funding from debt markets critical to the AI build-out, as lenders become pickier over corporate bonds.

But investors are now starting to ask harder questions about the bill for the AI build-out — and demanding evidence that the huge spending is actually adding value for shareholders, according to Dan Taylor, deputy chief investment officer and CIO equities, systematic at Man Group.

"As investors get choosier about where all this capital is going and when it might pay off, we think the market is likely to fragment well beyond the simple 'buy chipmakers, sell software' trade of the past two years," Taylor said.

"Anthropic may have got its IPO out the door just in time, but for the rest of the AI trade, the era of spending first and asking questions later seems to be over."

Bearish bond markets

Anthropic — which went public Nov. 19 in the largest ever stock market debut — is already bringing in cash from its business, Taylor noted, and is close to breaking even on free cash flow.

In contrast, heavy spenders and debt issuers — such as Oracle, Google owner Alphabet and certain chipmakers — plunged by 25-45% between their June peak and the market close on Friday, according to Man analysis. By comparison, Apple, which has sat out the AI spending arms race, was up almost 20%, Taylor observed in a Man Group note Tuesday.

Nvidia closed about 5.9% lower on Tuesday. Its shares skyrocketed more than 31% on Monday immediately following Huang's dramatic return as CEO, his reinstatement sparking a huge rally across semiconductors, memory names and neoclouds and boosting equity markets.

Matthew Rees, head of global bond strategies at L&G Asset Management, acknowledged bond markets have been consistently more bearish on Big Tech hyperscalers than equity markets. That stems partly from debt investors' broader outlook on the sector, but also from the sheer volume of issuance, Rees said.

"You're seeing BBB names like Oracle and SpaceX that are trading more like single B, partly because of concerns over fundamental credit quality, but also very much concerns about supply," Rees told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" Tuesday.

Accelerated AI-related borrowing is becoming a bigger share of U.S. corporate debt. PIMCO, citing Goldman Sachs data, expects the biggest AI companies to tap about $250 billion through bond sales this year. Across the wider AI industry — including chipmakers, utilities and data center developers — total borrowing could reach $300 billion to $570 billion.

'Not enough money to go round'

Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are now on track to spend more on capital projects than their businesses generated in cash in both 2026 and 2027, according to Man Group analysis. Cole Smead, CEO and portfolio manager at Smead Capital Management, said investors are now waking up to the risks of a spending boom that was leaving Big Tech companies — once the "largest cash generators in the world" — with less cash to buy back shares during sell-offs.

"There are vast capital needs in this AI story. The only problem is there's just not enough money to go around," Smead said.

He also questioned whether investors buying data center debt were being paid enough for the risks they were taking.

"They think they're getting 200-300 basis points over 10-year Treasury," Smead told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" before Huang returned on Monday.

"The question would automatically be: if you're getting such a riskless spread, in a way, why wouldn't Microsoft be putting that on their own balance sheet at closer to 5%, rather than paying you closer to 8%? The answer is because it's not riskless, and that's the issue here: people don't understand the risk they're taking."

Looking ahead, Taylor said the past week has demonstrated that a mega-IPO like Anthropic no longer lifts the whole market.

"We think the mega-cap tech spenders have room to rebound, yet doing so will likely require them to show more spending discipline and rebuild their free cash flow," Taylor said. "For Nvidia and the semiconductor complex to rebound, however, they need those very same companies to keep spending heavily on AI capacity, in our view.

"It is hard to see how both sides get what they need at the same time."

China's Shenzhou-24 carries Pakistan's first astronaut into space

China launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission on Wednesday carrying three astronauts to its Tiangong space station, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.

Beijing said it hopes the flight will strengthen ties with Islamabad, as the two countries mark 75 years of co-operation in space.

Speaking to reporters at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Ali said he was "carrying the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis".

The mission, which also comprises of commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, took off at 08:18 (00:18 GMT) from the Gobi desert. Minutes later, it was declared a "complete success".

While in space, the Shenzhou-24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like aerospace medicine, combustion and study the effects of space on living organisms.

They will also study how the space environment affects aging, with the hope of developing new ways to prevent and treat age-related vascular diseases.

Ali will conduct studies on photosynthesis in bacteria and the effects of radiation and microgravity - a very weak gravity in space - on seeds.

The former fighter pilot will return to Earth after a short stay, with two other Chinese crew members who have been at the space station since May.

Tang and Wu will spend six months at Tiangong space station along with Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, which lifted off in May this year. Zhu has been studying how the human body adapts to long periods in space.

The Shenzhou-24 is also a diplomatic moment for Beijing.

China has poured billions of dollars into its space programme and its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.

It is now keen to show the world that the station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.

This also comes at a time when Beijing is trying to establish itself as a major alternative to the US-led space programme, with a bold goal to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030.

For Pakistan, which does not have its own spacecraft to send astronauts to space, being invited to be a part of this mission is significant.

Ali and Khurram Dawood, the other candidate to reach the final stage in the Shenzhou-24 crew selection, were trained in China and had worked in Chinese space stations under the supervision of Chinese experts.

Mastering the Chinese language was one of his "biggest challenges", Ali said, according to Pakistani media.

A star's 'obliquity' likely has little impact on a given planet's habitability

A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumstellar disk that surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar-type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given star's initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

The angle between the spin axis of a star and the orbital axis of its planets—stellar obliquity—holds clues about how the spin-orbit orientations of stars and planets evolve throughout their lifetimes, Lauren Biddle, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told me via email.

In a paper accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal, and currently available on the arXiv preprint server, Biddle and her co-author, Brendan Bowler, compared stellar inclinations with orbital inclinations for 114 single sunlike stars.

Biddle and Bowler sampled 49 protoplanetary disk systems where planets were just beginning to form around their nascent stars. They also sampled 24 debris disk systems (stars circled by rings of gas, dust and rocky planetesimals).

The authors then sampled 21 warm Jupiter systems (where gas giant planets circle their parent stars on orbital periods that range between 10 and 100 days). And finally, they sampled 20 so-called hot Jupiter systems. Hot Jupiters were the first type of exoplanets found around sunlike stars and usually orbit their parent stars on insanely short orbits of less than 10 days, but at least one has been found to orbit its parent star in only 16 hours.

Yet as Biddle notes, the processes that drive changes in stellar obliquity could differ depending on a combination of how close a planet is to the central star and how old the planetary system actually is.

This work tests for signatures of obliquity evolution across "space" by comparing the spin-orbit angles of planetary systems across a range of orbital distances, and "time" by comparing systems over a range of ages, Biddle told me.

The results show that stellar obliquities are similar across orbital separation and age.

This suggests that after planets form, it is rare for their orbits to undergo large changes, and the changes that do happen are not detectable in the current data, says Biddle.

Not a lot of change

Some theories predict that orbital inclinations of planets could drastically change over time due to gravitational interactions with other planets or stars or, in the case of hot Jupiters, interactions from tidal forces with the host star, says Biddle. We don't see that in our data; instead, we find that the fraction of misaligned orbits in young planetary systems resembles that of older ones, she says.

By "stellar misalignment," Biddle means that the star's spin axis points in a different direction than the orbital axis of a planet. In contrast, a system is aligned when the star's equator lies in the same plane as the planet's orbit, like a spinning top placed at the center of a hula hoop.

It is misaligned when the star's spin axis is tipped relative to that plane, says Biddle. But because of observational limitations, we can only measure the lower limit of the angle between a star's tilt and the orbit's tilt, she says.

So, the true difference could actually be larger.

Thus far, however, large stellar obliquity changes appear to be uncommon. But Biddle notes that there is a major caveat in their data.

We deliberately chose single stars that are cooler and host giant transiting planets, says Biddle. We left out stars with close stellar companions, hot stars, small planets and nontransiting giant planets on wider orbits, so large tilts could be common in any of those, she says.

Stellar misalignments are out there

In practice, every system we classified as misaligned is tilted by at least 10 degrees, and on average the misaligned ones are tilted roughly 30 to 50 degrees, says Biddle.

But prior to the discovery of extrasolar planets, our understanding of these alignments was based entirely on the organization of the solar system, where planets are mostly aligned with the sun, with the large ones orbiting farther out, says Biddle. So, it came as a surprise when we discovered that giant close-in exoplanets with very misaligned orbits exist, she says.

The sun's spin axis, however, is tilted by about 6 degrees relative to the average orbital plane of the planets and dwarf planets, says Biddle.

Biddle doesn't know for certain if the sun's axis was tilted from the start.

But if we assume it started out aligned, there are several proposed explanations for how the sun could have become tilted, says Biddle. They include a past flyby of another star, tugs from an undiscovered distant planet, torques from stellar winds and even internal gravity waves, she says.

The bottom line?

There isn't evidence that stellar obliquity itself affects planetary habitability, says Biddle. But it does tell us about the history of planets' formation and where they eventually end up around the host star, which matters a lot when it comes to habitability, she says.

A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimerâs-like disease. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimerâs-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.

Researchers at the University of Sydney have created experimental nose drops that significantly improved learning and memory in older mice, bringing their performance back to levels seen in younger animals. The treatment also prevented severe memory decline in mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer's-like disease. Remarkably, the approach relies on mRNA technology similar to that used in COVID-19 vaccines.

The discovery, led by Professor Greg Neely at the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre, could open a new path toward treating conditions that affect the brain. Potential applications extend beyond Alzheimer's disease to other neurodegenerative disorders, stroke, traumatic brain injury, and rare genetic and developmental conditions.

"If we can proceed quickly to clinical trials in humans, this approach could represent a world-first non-invasive delivery system to treat Alzheimer's that bypasses the blood-brain barrier," Professor Neely said.

The idea behind the research has an unusual origin. The team drew inspiration from Daniel Keyes' science fiction story Flowers for Algernon, which explores the limits of human intelligence through experiments designed to increase intelligence in laboratory mice and people.

How mRNA Nose Drops Restore Youthful Memory

The treatment works by delivering messenger RNA (mRNA), a type of genetic instruction that tells cells how to produce specific proteins. These instructions are enclosed in tiny fat-based particles called lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which protect the mRNA and help it enter cells.

Once delivered through the nose, the mRNA instructs cells to manufacture therapeutic proteins capable of reaching the brain. In effect, the nasal tissue becomes a small drug-producing factory, creating substances that can support brain function.

"In aged mice, we saw learning and memory significantly increased, returning animal cognition to its youthful prime," Professor Neely said.

"What's exciting is that this was achieved with a simple non-invasive nasal delivery system that builds on the same underlying mRNA-LNP technology platform many people became familiar with during the COVID-19 pandemic."

The study, published in Advanced Science, used mRNA to stimulate production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). This naturally occurring protein helps neurons survive, form connections, and adapt as the brain learns and stores memories. Levels of BDNF tend to decline with aging and are also associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The results were striking. Older mice that received the nose drops performed about as well as young mice in standardized tests of working memory, spatial memory, and object recognition. These tests measure abilities such as remembering recently encountered information, navigating surroundings, and recognizing familiar objects. Untreated older animals showed the expected age-related deterioration in cognitive performance.

Nose Drops Prevent Alzheimer's-Like Memory Decline in Mice

To investigate whether the treatment might also protect against Alzheimer's disease, researchers turned to a widely used laboratory model known as 5XFAD mice. These animals carry genetic mutations that cause them to develop Alzheimer's-like brain changes and memory problems unusually early in life.

In this model, signs of Alzheimer's-related brain pathology can typically be detected by two months of age, with measurable cognitive decline appearing around four months.

The researchers began administering the BDNF-producing mRNA nose drops when the mice were two months old, around the time the disease-related changes first appeared. Treatment continued twice a week.

By four months of age, the treated mice showed no further cognitive decline, unlike the severe deterioration normally seen in this model. The findings suggest that supporting brain cells early in the disease process may help preserve cognitive abilities.

One of the most intriguing results was what the treatment did not do. Although memory and learning were protected, the researchers found no reduction in amyloid plaques, the abnormal protein deposits that accumulate in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease.

That distinction could be important because many existing Alzheimer's treatments aim to remove amyloid. The new approach instead appears to help neurons remain healthy and functional despite the presence of these deposits. If the same effect can eventually be demonstrated in people, the two treatment strategies might be used together.

"Current Alzheimer's treatments largely focus on clearing these amyloid plaques," Professor Neely said. "However, just under a third of Alzheimer's patients have serious plaques but do not suffer from dementia, and these patients show naturally higher BDNF levels, suggesting if we raise BDNF, it's possible to live with Alzheimer's disease pathology."

"Our approach seems to work not by clearing plaques but by supporting the health, survival and connectivity of neurons themselves. It raises the possibility these therapies could eventually work alongside each other."

Why it is here: original reporting, disaster management analysis

Queensland keeps learning disaster lessons.

After an early start to Queensland's storm season, with severe storms and flooding already affecting communities across the state, attention is once again turning to disaster preparedness and response.

When the season ends, reviews begin. Emergency services conduct debriefs; governments commission inquiries and researchers analyze what happened and why. These processes are designed to identify lessons and improve future responses.

Yet anyone who reads disaster reviews over time quickly notices a pattern. The same issues often reappear—fragmented decision-making, poor communication between organizations and insufficient engagement with communities.

Every storm season tests the resilience of communities, emergency services and government agencies. It also prompts an important question: Are we learning from previous disasters?

Institutional amnesia

The research shows disaster management agencies learn from major events and often implement significant changes in response.

However, it also shows that it is often more accurate to say that we fail to build institutional memory around our lessons.

We describe this as "institutional amnesia."

Rather than repeatedly failing to identify problems, governments often struggle to preserve knowledge and experience as people, priorities and structures change.

Research led by UQ found that several features of the public sector can contribute to this loss of organizational memory.

Staff turnover can result in expertise leaving with experienced employees. The movement of functions, resources and staff within government can disrupt established ways of working. Large knowledge-management systems may preserve information, but often without the context future staff will need to understand and apply it.

The consequences can be significant. Public servants spend time searching for lost information, organizations revisit problems they have already addressed, and valuable lessons become harder to access when new crises emerge.

As agencies review this storm season, the challenge is therefore not only identifying what worked and what did not. It is ensuring those insights remain accessible when the next major disaster occurs.

Social memory matters too

Institutional amnesia is not confined to government. Communities can also lose important knowledge about local risks and how best to respond when disaster strikes.

Population growth, housing mobility and changing employment patterns mean many people now live in places they have little historical connection to. New residents may be unfamiliar with the area's flood history or past disaster experiences, making it harder to interpret risk warnings and preparedness advice.

This can also reduce the effectiveness of planning tools such as flood maps. While the information remains available, it depends on people understanding local flood histories and recognizing how those risks relate to their own homes, businesses and daily activities.

More broadly, societies tend to focus on the future rather than the past. Innovation and change are often prioritized, while collective memories of previous disasters gradually fade.

The consequences become apparent when major events occur.

Research on the 2010–11 Queensland floods found that in some communities, memories of earlier flood events had weakened over time. As floodwaters rose, local knowledge about when to evacuate and how severe conditions could become was often overlooked or dismissed.

As a result, some residents were less prepared for the scale of the risk they faced.

Learning to remember

When this storm season ends, Queensland will once again review what happened and seek lessons for the future.

While this process is essential, if we take the same approach, we risk overlooking the ongoing challenge: ensuring those lessons endure.

In this crucial regard, within our government and communities, we cannot afford to overlook institutional amnesia.

For governments, that means building stronger systems for preserving knowledge as people and structures change. For communities, it means maintaining collective memory of local risks, even as populations grow and evolve.

The question is not whether Queensland can learn from disasters. It is whether we can remember what we have already learned.

New EU Bureaucracy Index: EU law has more than doubled since 2010

The new EU Bureaucracy Index measures the volume of EU law in force, and it shows a record high: At the end of 2025, the EU regulations and directives in force comprised around 47,600 standard pages, 118% more than in 2010. The volume of EU law has thus more than doubled in 15 years, and it continued to grow in 2025. The main drivers are sanctions regulations and new sets of rules in environmental, consumer and health law.

The EU Bureaucracy Index is compiled by professor Stefan Wagner of the University of Vienna, in collaboration with ESMT Berlin. It adds the European level to the Bureaucracy Index for German federal law, which ESMT published in March 2026.

The index covers all regulations and directives in force on Dec. 31 of a given year that were adopted jointly by the European Parliament and the Council or by the Council alone, each in its consolidated version. Legal acts of the European Commission are not included. As with the German index, volume is measured in standard pages of 1,500 characters each. The data come from Cellar, the database of the Publications Office of the European Union that underlies EUR-Lex.

The index does not count the number of legal acts. It measures their actual volume—that is, how much regulatory text applies at the EU level and ultimately affects companies, public administrations and citizens. Because EU law and federal law are measured in the same unit, developments at both levels can be compared.

If annexes such as lists, limit values and technical specifications are included along with the articles, EU law in force comprises around 90,800 standard pages (+85% since 2010). At the same time, there has been a shift in who makes the law: In 2000, 10% of the articles came from legal acts adopted jointly by Parliament and the Council; in 2025, the figure was 81%.

Eighteen of 20 policy areas have grown since 2010. Foreign and security policy saw the largest increase, with almost 12,900 additional standard pages. These are almost exclusively Council sanctions regulations with their lists of people, companies and goods.

In second place is law on the environment, consumer protection and health: Its volume has more than doubled, from around 4,300 to 9,800 standard pages. Outside sanctions law, no other area has added as many standard pages. This is driven above all by new sets of rules, for example on medical devices, renewable energy and industrial emissions. The Environmental Noise Directive alone grew by around 700 standard pages due to new calculation methods. Even when sanctions law is excluded, EU law has grown by 60% since 2010.

"EU law is growing almost twice as fast as German federal law," says Wagner. "Anyone who wants to reduce bureaucracy must also take the European level into account. Many of the obligations that companies in Germany complain about originate in Brussels. A national relief program alone will not solve the problem."

For companies in Germany, EU law and federal law add up. The Bureaucracy Index for federal law, which ESMT published this year, had already reached a record high. The volume of federal statutes in force rose from 24,765 standard pages in 2010 to 40,270 in 2025. Commercial law grew the most: 1,542 standard pages were added between 2022 and 2026 (+16.5%), more than in any previous period since the analysis began.

The articles of the EU regulations and directives in force alone now comprise roughly as many standard pages as all federal statutes combined. Including annexes, EU law is more than twice as extensive, and it is growing significantly faster.

The index does not assess whether individual regulations make sense. It measures the volume of the law in force. Sanctions law in particular is politically intended, and its extensive lists drive the figures up. However, the index shows where regulation has increased particularly sharply over the past 15 years, providing a basis for a targeted debate on reducing the burden of bureaucracy at the European level.

Will there be a White Christmas this year?

Christmas Day is a month away and as the festive season approaches you may start to wonder - could 2026 be a 'white Christmas'?

The likelihood is actually higher than you might imagine.

Over the past 65 years, there have been 41 white Christmases, meaning we are more likely than not to see one somewhere in the UK.

Forecasting the chances of a month ahead of the big day is a bit like staring into a crystal ball - but are there any early omens of snow on the festive horizon?

How do we define a white Christmas?

For a Christmas to be officially declared as 'white', a single snowflake needs to be recorded falling at any point during 25 December, at any of the Met Office's network of around 300 weather stations.

It means there doesn't have to be a thick covering of snow on the ground to qualify.

Indeed, the landscape could be beautifully festive and white with lying snow, but if no new snow falls on Christmas Day it cannot technically be called a white Christmas.

The last widespread white Christmas was in 2010, when snow fell at 19% of measuring stations and a significant 83% of stations reported snow lying on the ground.

Every year from 2020 to 2023 was officially a white Christmas, however very few places actually reported settling snow.

Are there signs we could have a white Christmas in the UK this year?

A number of factors will influence the UK's weather in the run-up to the festive season.

A major one is the record-breaking El NiÃ±o which is, scientists predict, approaching its peak in the Pacific.

El NiÃ±o's strongest impacts tend to be felt close to where the phenomenon occurs, in the tropical Pacific, but the energy it releases into the atmosphere can send ripples through weather patterns across the globe.

In the UK, the impacts tend to be subtle and unreliable.

Strong El NiÃ±o events can increase the odds of wet and stormy weather during the late autumn and early winter, and some studies suggest they can raise the chances of colder weather later in the season - but the evidence from past El NiÃ±os is decidedly mixed.

And this is far from the only factor driving our weather.

- Will El NiÃ±o and the polar vortex bring snow to the UK this winter?

- Stormy autumn, cold winter - how might El NiÃ±o affect the UK weather?

Earlier in November the winds of the stratospheric polar vortex weakened and reversed, marking the earliest sudden stratospheric warming event on record.

This phenomenon tends to occur much later in winter and can - but doesn't always - weaken the jet stream, increasing the chance of cold northerly or easterly winds.

Occurring so early in the season, the effects this time are harder to quantify. It is not known what - if any - impact it will have on the weather over the weeks ahead.

The latest predictions from scientists at the Met Office, external, taking these and other factors into account, suggest there could be an increased likelihood of colder and drier-than-average conditions during the winter months of December, January and February.

However this only represents an increased probability of these conditions and - even if this occurs across the season as a whole - there are still very likely to be shorter-term periods of milder, wetter weather.

When will we know for sure if Christmas will be white?

It is often tricky to accurately forecast snow in the UK, even a day or two in advance.

Snow requires just the right combination of cold air and moisture, and small changes in either of these elements can mean predicted snow actually falls as rain or vice versa.

It goes without saying that longer range snow forecasts are even more challenging and with Christmas still a month away it is impossible to offer precise predictions.

You can keep up to date with the latest forecast by checking BBC Weather online and the app.

Extinct, long-legged grasshoppers walked on water alongside dinosaurs

Amber fossils preserve tiny paddles on the lower leg that could have powered each stroke

Nearly 100 million years ago, spindly legged grasshoppers may have scooted across water like modern day water striders. The clues are in the fossilized insects’ legs and feet.

Special hairs and leaf-shaped leg adornments, exquisitely preserved in amber, suggest the insects — members of a newfound family of insects — could balance and slide around on surface tension, researchers report November 24 in Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The discovery suggests at least three insect groups evolved independently to move across water.

Paleontologist Chunpeng Xu and his colleagues first encountered the strange insects while studying a collection of 99-million-year-old amber. Frozen in time were three pieces of amber containing wingless grasshoppers with short bodies and incredibly long, skinny legs. Due to their unorthodox body shape, Xu didn’t recognize them as grasshoppers at first and thought they might be harvestmen or stick insects.

“I was genuinely amazed,” says Xu, of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Paleontology in China. “They are among the most bizarre insects.”

Under the microscope, two details stood out: Front legs with water repellant hairs and rear lower legs with leaf-shaped paddlelike structures. Estimates of the insects’ weight show they could have ridden on the water’s surface tension, with help from the repellant hairs on their legs and their spread-out footprint across the surface of the water. And the paddlelike lower legs would have propelled them forward.

The researchers named the insects Hydrelcana zhangi, placing them in the new family Hydrelcanidae.

“Walking on water is a pretty rare skill in nature,” Xu says. Until now, only two insect groups were known to have evolved to live on the water’s surface: water striders and their kin, and a similar looking but unrelated, long extinct family called Chresmodidae.

The grasshoppers had a different gait from other water-walking insects. The common pond skater (Gerris lacustris), by comparison, rows with its middle limbs.

And whereas modern water-walking insects are predators and scavengers, the ancient grasshoppers were also probably herbivorous, given their mouthparts and lack of claws. The researchers found nine of them preserved in the same amber chunk, suggesting the insects may have gathered in large numbers to feed. It’s possibly the earliest record of such swarming behavior in grasshoppers or crickets, the team says.

Early-stage breast cancer gains first newly approved hormone therapy in more than 20 years

For the first time in more than two decades, the FDA has approved a new hormone therapy for early-stage breast cancer, marking a monumental shift in how the most common form of the disease is treated.

Estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer makes up about 70% of all diagnoses. Known generically as giredestrant, this once-daily pill works by finding and destroying the estrogen receptors in breast tissue, effectively starving any remaining cancer cells of the hormone fuel they need to grow.

Following surgery, patients typically take daily hormone-blocking pills for up to 10 years to prevent the cancer from returning. However, standard therapies often come with harsh side effects that cause many women to abandon their treatment early, leaving them vulnerable to a relapse.

Better protection with fewer side effects

This historic FDA approval introduces a highly effective, easier-to-tolerate alternative that is poised to change the standard of care. According to landmark data from the lidERA trial, published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology, this new treatment significantly improves disease-free survival and reduces the risk of the cancer spreading to other organs (metastatic disease). Crucially, this benefit was proven in both premenopausal and postmenopausal women.

"The approval of giredestrant is practice-changing as it is a better option over standard endocrine therapy for adjuvant treatment of breast cancer. It is better tolerated and has better efficacy as shown in the lidERA trial," said Madhurima Anne, M.D., FACP, chief of hematology/oncology at Hackensack Meridian Ocean University Medical Center and medical oncologist at Jersey Shore University Medical Center.

"For over 20 years, oncologists have had to counsel women through the difficult side effects of standard hormone therapies, knowing that if they stop taking their daily pill, their risk of relapse increases. Having giredestrant as a highly effective, easier-to-tolerate alternative is an absolute game-changer. It means we can finally protect our patients from a recurrence without asking them to sacrifice their daily quality of life," said Donna McNamara, M.D., breast medical oncologist, Hackensack Meridian John Theurer Cancer Center at Hackensack University Medical Center.

Why it is here: Important public health issue with clear explanation and context

A doctor's take on the US losing measles elimination status

For many physicians of my generation, measles was a disease we rarely—or never—saw in practice. That was a sign of how well vaccination and public health efforts had worked.

Now, with the United States having lost its measles elimination status, I'm concerned that I may soon face a disease I never expected to encounter as a doctor.

Measles is spreading again, and this highly contagious virus can quickly reach communities where vaccination protection has slipped.

Measles elimination never meant the virus was gone for good. It meant we had stopped the constant spread of measles in the United States.

Sometimes, cases would come in from other countries, but we were able to stop them from spreading widely. Now, losing that status means the same chain of measles spread has continued in the U.S. for at least a year.

Not every community is seeing cases, but we can't assume measles will be contained without effort.

Measles is much more than just a rash and fever. It can lead to serious problems like pneumonia, swelling of the brain, hospital stays and, in rare cases, death, according to The New England Journal of Medicine.

Babies, pregnant people, children under age 5, adults over age 20, people with weak immune systems and those who can't get vaccinated are at the highest risk.

The virus spreads through the air and can hang around in a room even after the sick person has left, so even a short exposure can put someone at risk if they aren't protected.

The best way to protect ourselves is simple: Get vaccinated, stay informed and act quickly when there's a risk.

Two doses of the MMR vaccine work well for most people. If you're not sure if you or your child is up to date, check with your doctor or local health department. Communities should make it easy for everyone to get vaccinated and answer questions with respect.

Shaming families or turning this into a political issue doesn't help anyone.

Doctors and nurses have an important job, too. We need to watch for symptoms, ask about travel or possible exposure and call ahead before sending someone with suspected measles into a waiting room.

This helps protect other patients and gives public health teams time to act.

If you think you've been exposed, call your health care provider or health department for advice before going in.

This is time-sensitive because after an exposure to measles, the MMR vaccine should be given within 72 hours and immune globulin within six days, The New England Journal of Medicine states.

Losing measles elimination status is a serious setback, but we can fix it.

We got rid of ongoing measles before by keeping vaccination rates high and working together in public health. We can do it again.

The real lesson is that vaccines work, but only if enough people get them. Every community needs strong vaccination coverage, not just the country as a whole.

Drones could soon fly blood, defibrillators and medicine to patients

Paramedics in one Florida county may soon be able to call in a drone to bring blood to a patient who's bleeding heavily.

Hillsborough County says the system is the nation's first of its kind, The Washington Post reported. It should launch within weeks, starting with a 70-square-mile (181-square-kilometer) area.

Paramedics will order temperature-controlled whole blood through a phone app. The aim is for blood to arrive within 3.5 minutes.

County officials said the drones could help people hurt in car crashes, shootings or stabbings, as well as women with severe bleeding after childbirth. For some of these patients, waiting for a transfusion at the hospital could be too late.

Archer First Response Systems runs the blood program and began flying emergency drones in two Florida counties in May 2024. So far, its drones have answered 15 emergency calls, founder and CEO Gordon Folkes told The Post.

Those drones carry ready-made kits that can include an automated external defibrillator (AED). This portable device reads the heart's rhythm and, if needed, shocks it back into a steady beat.

Kits may also hold tourniquets, Narcan for opioid overdose, albuterol for asthma attacks and epinephrine for severe allergic reactions.

In one case, a drone lowered an AED to a woman whose husband had collapsed. "She got the AED pads on the chest about four minutes before ground units even arrived on the scene," Folkes said.

The device spotted a heart rhythm a shock can't fix, and he died.

Still, speed matters in cardiac arrest. Without a shock, a person's odds of survival fall 7% to 10% with each passing minute, the American Heart Association estimates.

"In cardiac arrest, getting a defibrillator to someone quickly is absolutely crucial," Dr. Robson Gilmour, a U.K. resident doctor who studies drone transport of donor organs, told The Post.

In western Sweden, AED drones are now part of many emergency responses. They cover about 15% of the region's population, local officials told The Post.

Programs are popping up elsewhere, too. In July, Cleveland Clinic teamed up with drone company Zipline on what The Post called a first-of-its-kind program to deliver prescriptions by drone.

Yet medical drones haven't caught on widely in the United States. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) rules generally require drones to stay where the pilot can see them, Gilmour said. Waivers exist, but they don't easily support a large, everyday delivery network, he added.

Those limits also slow efforts to fly donor organs. In 2019, a drone carried a kidney less than 3 miles (4.8 kilometers) across Baltimore for a successful transplant.

Gilmour expects blood, lab samples and medicines to become routine first. They're more frequent and easier to fit into today's health systems, he explained.

In parts of sub-Saharan Africa with rough roads, drones already deliver blood, vaccines and medicines routinely.

"I'd imagine there are plenty of similar situations in rural parts of the United States where drones could make a real difference," Gilmour said.

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Insight into adolescent brain development with clear explanation

Disrupting a developing brain circuit in adolescence may have lasting social effects

Adolescence is often described as a turbulent period of life marked by growing independence, changing social relationships and unpredictable shifts in behavior. According to researchers, tweens' and teens' behavioral changes reflect a brain that is still actively developing, yet scientists know surprisingly little about the neural mechanisms that shape social behavior during this critical stage of life.

Studying how the adolescent brain develops has become increasingly important, especially because many psychiatric disorders first emerge during the teenage years.

"We don't know much about the adolescent brain. If we compare it to early postnatal life, or infant development, we know so much about that. But adolescence, well, we're still trying to get it," said Laurence Coutellier, an associate professor of behavioral neuroscience in The Ohio State University Department of Psychology.

New mouse study findings from Coutellier's lab suggest that a brain pathway known as the prefrontal cortex–ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR) circuit undergoes important development during adolescence and may play a key role in social motivation. The circuit sends signals from the prefrontal cortex—the brain's command center—to the ventral striatum, a region associated with reward processing, motivation and pleasure.

Lead author Katrina Lin, a doctoral candidate and graduate research assistant in Coutellier's lab, recently presented preliminary findings on a poster at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience. The study showed that mice whose activity in this pathway was temporarily inhibited during adolescence were less motivated to socialize as adults. The same intervention in adult mice did not produce this effect.

Previously, Coutellier's lab examined how changes in PFC-vSTR circuits during adolescence help shape social behaviors. For this study, the researchers wanted to know if adolescence represents a particularly sensitive period for development of the pathway and whether disrupting that process would have lasting effects on behavior.

Coutellier's lab has studied the prefrontal cortex, the brain region associated with functions like working memory, attention, decision-making, impulse control and social behavior, for more than a decade. "What's interesting with this region is that it's the last brain region to mature," she said. When an adolescent acts impulsively or displays inflexible thinking patterns, it's normal, because the prefrontal cortex doesn't fully mature until around age 25, she explained.

Unlike humans, whose adolescence lasts for the better part of a decade, mice have a short adolescence of about three weeks, which allows researchers to study social activity patterns across the animal's life span.

To establish a baseline of behavior in mice by age, Coutellier's team first ran a social interaction test, placing two mice that hadn't met before in the same cage and filming their interactions.

"I always say it's like two dogs in a park. They start sniffing each other. They're careful at first, and then they go into a different type of sniffing behavior," she said. The researchers predicted that adolescent mice would show more social motivation than adult mice, and that's exactly what they found.

"In humans it's the same," Coutellier said. "A teenager loves to hang out with their friends, and they will seek this interaction. As adults, we will be more careful. We don't approach a stranger just like that, and we'll be more cautious about the way we interact. There's still a strong social motivation, which is necessary for us to have social relationships, but there is less of it."

In other words, the drive to seek out meaningful relationships with peers appears to be hardwired in the adolescent brain.

Coutellier emphasized that animal studies can't fully replicate human behavior, but allow researchers to manipulate specific brain circuits and see how changes affect behavior.

To test whether the PFC-vSTR circuit drives social development, the team used a technique to turn specific neurons on or off in both male and female mice. When researchers quieted activity in the circuit during adolescence, the mice grew up to be less socially motivated as adults. By contrast, quieting the same circuit in adult mice caused only a temporary dip in social investigation while the intervention was active, suggesting that adolescence may be a uniquely important period for wiring social behavior.

"We found that actually, yes, if we prevent the maturation of the frontal circuit to the striatum, when mice reach adulthood they have impaired social motivation," Coutellier said.

Learning how these circuits typically develop could help researchers better understand what happens when their development deviates. Many psychiatric disorders, including depression and schizophrenia, first appear during adolescence, Coutellier said, and they often present with social challenges or withdrawal.

She's especially interested in examining specific environmental factors that may influence how brain circuits mature. For example: "We can try to study what happens when our mice don't get to socialize, and we can think about what happened during COVID-19, when teenagers were told to stay home and stop socializing to be safe. How did that impact this developmental trajectory of the social circuits?" she said.

In addition, the lab has been studying behavior in mice that resembles traits observed in people with schizophrenia.

"Mice do not have schizophrenia. Mice do not have depression. But there are some symptoms that we can try to assess," she said. "Like social withdrawal or cognitive deficits. We're trying to understand what genetic and environmental factors can make these symptoms arise at the time of adolescence—not before, and not in adulthood, but during that sensitive period of development."

England shows widest socioeconomic gap in frailty among 31 countries

Older adults from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds experience greater levels of frailty, with England showing the biggest gap between socioeconomic groups among the 31 countries studied.

The research, led by King's College London, indicates that lower socioeconomic status is associated with a more rapid progression of frailty over time, with the gap between socioeconomic groups becoming substantially bigger as people age.

The study, published in BMC Medicine, examined over 71,703 people across 31 countries, including the United States, China and multiple European countries.

Frailty was measured on a scale from 0 to 100, based on the proportion of health problems and functional limitations a person experienced, with higher scores indicating greater frailty.

At age 50, those in the lowest socioeconomic group had frailty scores nearly seven points higher than people in the highest socioeconomic group, who were classified by high levels of income, educational attainment and occupation.

By age 80, this gap had widened to around 12 points, suggesting that socioeconomic inequalities in frailty become more pronounced with age.

The researchers identified social and physical inactivity as the two main drivers of the higher levels of frailty in people with lower socioeconomic status, suggesting that there are strong links between frailty and social habits.

The findings of this study are consistent with broader evidence of substantial health inequalities in England.

Dongfeng Tang, first author of the study and a final-year Ph.D. student from the Department of Primary Care and Data Science at King's College London, said, "We were surprised to see that England has the steepest socioeconomic inequalities in frailty out of all of the countries we studied. While we cannot establish exactly why this is the case, the findings highlight the importance of addressing the wider social and economic conditions that shape healthy aging.

"Additionally, our research indicates that someone's socioeconomic status could put them at higher risk of becoming frail, and this disadvantage could accumulate across the life course. Lifestyle habits, such as being socially connected and staying active, could offer an opportunity to intervene to improve someone's health outcomes."

Frailty is usually characterized by difficulty with multiple daily activities, such as walking or getting dressed, and a reduced physiological reserve, so a person cannot easily recover from a setback such as a minor illness.

Frailty can be associated with increased risks of disability, dependency, hospitalization and mortality. Older adults living with frailty have been shown to contribute to a large share of emergency department visits, unplanned acute hospital admissions and extended hospital lengths of stay.

Identifying if someone is at risk of frailty early allows for targeted interventions that can prolong their independence and keep them healthier for longer.

The research combined data from a frailty score, which included 27 different areas of someone's health such as self-reported chronic conditions and cognitive performance, with their socioeconomic status.

Two indicators were used to measure socioeconomic status: education level and total household wealth. The research grouped people's highest level of education into three groups: primary, secondary and tertiary (university) education.

Total household wealth was calculated as the sum of all wealth components (residence, business, vehicles and savings accounts), excluding debts or loans.

Lifestyle factors included smoking, heavy drinking, physical inactivity and social inactivity.

Matthew O'Connell, senior lecturer in population health sciences at King's College London and the senior author of the study, said, "It is highly concerning that people from lower socioeconomic groups had higher levels of frailty across all countries studied, with the greatest inequalities in England.

"More encouragingly, the increasing role of lifestyle factors at older ages suggests increasing physical and social activities in mid to later life might help to reduce frailty at older ages. This is something that could be encouraged for everyone as they age and could be a targeted intervention for groups potentially at higher risk."

Why it is here: Policy impact on healthcare access with clear explanation

Prior authorization limits help expand opioid addiction treatment where approvals were a frequent roadblock, study finds

State laws limiting prior authorization requirements for opioid use disorder medications were associated with increased buprenorphine use in Medicaid, but only in states where those requirements were frequent barriers to access, according to a new study led by University of Michigan researchers.

Published in JAMA Network Open, the research found that in those states (Arkansas, Illinois and Wisconsin), the laws were associated with roughly a 19% increase in the monthly rate of patients receiving buprenorphine and a 34% increase in the rate of patients starting it, compared with baseline levels. Patients also received their prescriptions nearly a day sooner, and prescription claim rejections because of prior authorization fell by about 7.5 percentage points.

In the other 10 jurisdictions that enacted laws, where those rejections were less common, the researchers found no statistically significant associations with any study outcome. Across all 13 jurisdictions combined, the laws were not associated with statistically significant changes in buprenorphine dispensing, treatment initiation or the time between prescribing and dispensing.

"While prior authorization requirements may promote appropriate care in some situations, our findings suggest that reducing these administrative barriers can help more people receive buprenorphine treatment in settings where prior authorization is common," said Thuy Nguyen, the study's first author and an associate professor of health management and policy at the University of Michigan School of Public Health.

Removing one barrier among many

Medicaid is the largest financing source for opioid use disorder treatment in the United States, according to the study. Prior authorization, the requirement to secure an insurer's approval before it covers a medication, can delay medication treatment, making it an important target for efforts to improve access.

The findings suggest that limiting prior authorization may help expand treatment access when those requirements commonly stand in patients' way. Where they are uncommon, other barriers may need greater attention, including limited access to pharmacies that stock buprenorphine and stigma surrounding opioid use disorder and its treatment.

"Buprenorphine is a highly effective treatment for opioid use disorder and can be prescribed in routine office-based care," said Nguyen, who is also a member of the University of Michigan Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation. She noted that expanding access to this lifesaving medication is critically important as potent opioids continue to drive overdose risk.

About the study

The researchers analyzed two national pharmacy databases from 2014 through 2020, including nearly 12.7 million dispensed buprenorphine prescriptions for more than 652,000 Medicaid patients ages 15 to 64. They compared changes in 13 jurisdictions that implemented laws limiting prior authorization from 2015 to 2019 with changes in 25 states that did not. The study focused on immediate-release buprenorphine and on laws implemented before the COVID-19 pandemic, and it did not measure clinical outcomes such as overdoses.

FDA approves bezuclastinib in combination with sunitinib as new second-line therapy for patients with GIST

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a combination of bezuclastinib plus sunitinib as second-line therapy after first-line treatment with imatinib for adults with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) based on evidence from the phase 3 PEAK study led by Dana-Farber Cancer Institute showing that the combination outperformed standard therapy with sunitinib alone.

"With today's FDA approval of bezuclastinib in combination with sunitinib, we have a new standard-of-care treatment following imatinib for patients with GIST," said Andrew Wagner, M.D., Ph.D., deputy chief medical officer and senior physician in the Center for Sarcoma and Bone Oncology at Dana-Farber. "This approval represents a major step forward for the GIST community and reflects the tireless progress made in improving the lives of people living with this disease."

GIST, which is diagnosed in 4,000 to 5,000 people in the U.S. each year, occurs when abnormal cells form in the gastrointestinal tract—the stomach, small intestine and large intestine. In the vast majority of GISTs, the tumor cells have a mutation in the KIT gene, which causes the cells to divide uncontrollably.

Evidence supporting the use of KIT inhibitors such as first-line imatinib and second-line sunitinib to treat advanced GIST emerged from Dana-Farber research. While KIT inhibitors have improved outcomes, tumors still develop resistance, typically by developing additional KIT mutations.

Bezuclastinib inhibits common primary and secondary resistance mutations in advanced KIT-mutant GIST. The pivotal phase 3 PEAK study enrolled 413 patients with advanced GIST who had received prior therapy with imatinib and who were randomized to receive either bezuclastinib plus sunitinib or sunitinib alone. The combination, which was well tolerated by patients, reduced the risk of progression or death by 50%. The overall response rate also improved from 26% with monotherapy to 46% with the combination.

"The PEAK study results support the biologic rationale that more complete inhibition of the spectra of KIT mutations in a given patient can provide better and more durable outcomes than using a single drug," Wagner said. "It is exciting to see this combination replace sunitinib alone, which has been the standard for about 20 years."

General-purpose speech models work out of the box, but the moment they encounter industry jargon, regional accents, proprietary product names, or a fixed voice, they start "hallucinating" or going off-key. Below, we break it down in engineering deployment order, providing reproducible configurations for both ASR and TTS pipelines.

I. First, Clarify What You're Fine-Tuning

• ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition): Audio → Text. Representatives: Whisper, Fun-ASR-Nano, Qwen-Audio, etc.

• TTS / Voice Cloning (Speech Synthesis): Text + Reference Audio → Audio. Representatives: GPT-SoVITS, Qwen3-TTS, ChatTTS, VITS family.

• End-to-End Speech Large Models: Unified modeling of audio tokens ↔ text tokens. During fine-tuning, usually only the adapter or LLM intermediate layers are modified.

For model selection, don't jump straight to full-parameter fine-tuning. For <100 hours of domain data, prioritize LoRA / Adapter / only unfreezing the decoder; consider full-parameter tuning only when data exceeds 10,000 hours.

II. Data Preparation: Determines 80% of the Ceiling

ASR Data Checklist (JSONL or two-column CSV)

{"audio": "data/001.wav", "sr": 16000, "duration": 6.2,

"text": "Send me the X7-Pro spec sheet via email", "domain": "erp_order", "speaker": "sp_023"}

Hard rules:

• Unified 16 kHz mono. Use the model's built-in log_mel_spectrogram; don't calculate mel manually with librosa.

• Single clip ≤ 30 s (Whisper window); cut long audio at natural pauses.

• Trim leading/trailing silence, double-label + spot-check, manually verify alignment for 10 random clips—misalignment is more fatal than poor hyperparameters.

• Domain data : General data ≈ 7:3 mix, to prevent "forgetting how to speak."

• 10 hours is the starting point; 30+ hours brings a performance leap; for <10 hours, freeze the encoder and only train the decoder.

TTS / Cloning Data

• 1–30 min of clean dry vocals per speaker for zero-shot trial; 1.5–3 hours of fine-tuning is needed to stably beat zero-shot similarity.

• Long audio → UVR to remove BGM → cut into 3–10 s segments → ASR for labeling → manual correction of typos (typos = voice drift).

• Annotation format: audio|speaker|lang|text, use zh/en/ja/ko/yue for lang.

• For speaker embedding, don't use a single reference clip; take the centroid of 64 embeddings, boosting cosine similarity from ~0.7 to 0.85+.

III. ASR Fine-Tuning: Two Paths — Whisper & Fun-ASR

Path A: Whisper (Seq2SeqTrainer + LoRA)

Key configuration

model = WhisperForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained("openai/whisper-medium")

LoRA only attached to attention q/k/v

peft_config = LoraConfig(r=16, target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj"],

lora_dropout=0.05, bias="none")

Small data: freeze encoder, only train decoder + LoRA

for p in model.model.encoder.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False

• lr: Full-parameter 1e-5, LoRA 1e-4; warmup 500–2000 steps + cosine decay

• bf16/fp16 + gradient checkpointing, effective batch 16–64 (use grad accum to reach)

• SpecAugment: use conservatively (don't mask too aggressively when domain data is scarce)

• Metrics: Validation set WER / CER, early stop if no drop for 3 consecutive epochs

• Vocabulary expansion: After adding new domain tokens to tokenizer, train embedding with a higher lr separately; don't let random initialization drag down convergence

Practical reference: 20h medical dictation fine-tuned on medium, terminology WER 12% → 4.5%; 4h Icelandic fine-tuned on turbo, 18% → 6%.

Path B: Fun-ASR-Nano (ChatML format, full-parameter friendly)

Convert data to ChatML:

{"messages":[

{"role":"system","content":"You are a helpful assistant."},

{"role":"user","content":"Speech transcription:!./audio/001.wav"},

{"role":"assistant","content":"Order has generated a sales order"}

]}

Freezing strategy based on data volume:

• <1000 h: Only train audio_adaptor

• <5000 h: Train audio_encoder + audio_adaptor

• >10000 h: Full-parameter

After training: run decode.py → whisper_mix_normalize.py for inverse normalization → compute-wer.

IV. TTS / Voice Cloning Fine-Tuning: GPT-SoVITS & Qwen3-TTS

GPT-SoVITS Pipeline (WebUI is the easiest)

- Split long audio (3–10 s)

- Auto-transcribe with faster-whisper / funasr

- Manually proofread text (this step determines success or failure)

- Format → First train SoVITS (8–16 epochs) → Then train GPT (15–20 epochs)

- Output xxx_e10.ckpt + xxx.pth packaged as a voice directory; no need to pass reference audio during inference

Pitfalls:

• OOM → Reduce batch size or enable is_half

• Metallic sound → Use v4 (native 48 kHz); v3 has upsampling artifacts

• One audio clip only learns one "speaking state"; if trained on singing, it will output singing

Qwen3-TTS class (RVQ multi-codebook)

• Loss = talker loss (codebook 0) + 0.3 × sub-talker loss (layers 1–15)

• lr ≤ 1e-5, warmup + cosine; flat lr causes early overshooting and late overfitting

• Bake speaker embedding centroid into checkpoint; TTFA reduced from ~154 ms (ICL) to ~130 ms

Preventing Catastrophic Forgetting (Multi-speaker incremental training)

• Decouple speaker encoder, freeze backbone and only train embedding / adapter

• LoRA per-speaker stores matrices, without touching base weights

• Replay: Mix in 5–10% old speaker samples, or use generative pseudo-replay

• EWC penalizes key parameter drift

V. Hyperparameter Quick Reference (Single A100/H100 starting point)

item.description:
