I am Orlando Ezequiel Salazar Cruz, a Computer Systems Engineering student at the Instituto Tecnológico Superior de Calkiní (ITESCAM) in Campeche, Mexico. Throughout my coursework and personal projects, I have spent most of my time building web interfaces with Angular and TypeScript, along with backend services using Python and FastAPI.

When you are studying software engineering, distributed systems can easily feel like something reserved for senior engineers running large cloud clusters. You read about service discovery, retries, event-driven messaging, and fault tolerance, and it is easy to assume you need complex infrastructure before you can even start building.

Discovering Dapr (Distributed Application Runtime) gave me a much clearer way to understand distributed applications. It also gave me a realistic entry point into open source software, showing me that your first contributions do not have to be massive runtime features to be useful to other developers.

What Dapr Is and Why It Exists

Dapr is an open-source, portable, event-driven runtime designed to help developers build resilient distributed applications across cloud and edge environments. Instead of requiring your application code to import vendor-specific SDKs or manage infrastructure clients directly, Dapr runs alongside your application—commonly as a sidecar process—and exposes standard HTTP and gRPC APIs.

Modern applications rarely run as a single process talking to one database. Even a small microservice architecture usually needs to persist state, publish and subscribe to events, call other services, read secrets, or coordinate multi-step workflows. Without a consistent runtime abstraction, each service ends up repeating boilerplate code for retries, timeouts, serialization, and client setup—often tightly coupled to one specific database, message broker, or cloud provider.

Dapr separates what your application wants to do (such as saving state or publishing an event) from how the underlying infrastructure performs that operation (such as Redis, PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, or cloud-managed services). Your code talks to the local Dapr sidecar over HTTP or gRPC, and Dapr handles the interaction with the configured component.

Problems Dapr Solves in Distributed Systems

Distributed systems introduce failure modes that do not exist in a single-process application. Network requests fail, downstream services restart or slow down, and partial outages happen regularly.

Dapr helps reduce several common problems in microservice and distributed architectures:

- Infrastructure coupling: Switching from one state store or pub/sub broker to another can be handled through Dapr component configuration instead of rewriting application logic across multiple services, provided the new component supports the required capabilities.

- Language lock-in: Because Dapr exposes standard HTTP and gRPC APIs alongside official SDKs, services written in different languages—such as Python, TypeScript, Go, or .NET—can work together using the same runtime model.

- Repetitive operational logic: Writing retry policies, timeouts, and observability hooks from scratch in every service is repetitive and error-prone. A sidecar runtime standardizes how services interact with external building blocks.

- Local-to-cloud consistency: You can run Dapr locally during development and use similar component abstractions in production environments without changing how your application calls Dapr APIs.

Core Building Blocks of Dapr

One of the easiest ways to learn Dapr is through its building blocks. Each building block solves a specific distributed systems task while keeping your application code focused on business logic.

Service Invocation

Service Invocation lets one service call another reliably using a Dapr app ID instead of hardcoding hostnames, ports, or network locations. Dapr handles discovery and routing through the sidecar layer, making service-to-service communication simpler across environments.

State Management

State Management provides a consistent API for saving, retrieving, updating, and deleting key-value state without coupling your code to a specific database driver. It also supports features like optimistic concurrency control (ETags), where supported by the state store, so multiple service instances can update shared state safely.

Publish and Subscribe

Publish and Subscribe (pub/sub) decouples event producers from event consumers using topics. A service publishes an event to a topic without needing to know which downstream services are subscribed or how many instances are running.

Bindings

Bindings let your application react to external events (input bindings) or trigger external systems (output bindings) through a uniform interface—such as cron schedules, queues, storage buckets, or messaging systems—without writing custom integration code for each external service.

Secrets Management

Secrets Management gives applications a standard way to retrieve sensitive values—such as API keys, database passwords, or tokens—from a configured secret store instead of hardcoding secrets or writing custom secret-loading logic in every service.

Workflows

Workflows allow you to orchestrate long-running, stateful, multi-step processes across services and activities. If a process spans several steps or encounters transient failures and restarts, Dapr Workflows tracks execution state so the workflow can resume reliably.

item.description:

The Rust team has released Rust 1.100.0, the language's first three-digit stable version, with a release that finally lands the never type after a decade of work. Announced on 12 November 2026, the release also stabilises the core of the custom allocator API, introduces a DropGuard helper, and gives Cargo opt-in dependency cooldowns and warnings for unused dependencies.

The headline is the stabilisation of !, the canonical uninhabited type for computations that never return a value, such as panic!(), return or an endless loop. Although functions have long used it as a return type, naming it elsewhere, for instance writing Result<T, !> to describe an operation that cannot fail, took ten years and five failed stabilisation attempts to land. The release also makes std::convert::Infallible an alias for !, which is what the type was always intended to be, so existing APIs using Infallible now accept ! transparently.

To make that alias work, the team shipped a small breaking change for the 2015, 2018 and 2021 editions, flipping the never-type fallback from () to ! and matching behaviour already introduced in Rust 2024. The release notes describe the impact as largely unnoticeable but warn that more code may be flagged as unreachable. Developers hitting issues on upgrade are advised to update dependencies first, since fixes for widely used crates have already been published.

The core of the long-awaited allocator_api is also now stable, letting library authors define custom allocators used with Vec and Box through the new Allocator trait. This forms the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. Critics on the internals forum have argued that Rust still lacks Zig's granular control over allocation because the current design cannot support inline storage, with moves invalidating internal pointers, but the stabilised core is seen as a workable starting point for broader collections support.

On the Hacker News release post, one user noted that some of the changes weren’t mentioned in the blog post for the release:

This release is so big that multiple useful stabilized API aren't event mentioned in the blog post like:

- bool::toggle() https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/primitive.bool.html#met...

- Box::map() https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/boxed/struct.Box.html#m...

- str::trim_prefix(), str::trim_suffix, Path::trim_prefix()

The new global-min-publish-age setting holds back newly published versions by a configurable window, an opt-in defence against malicious crate releases:

[registry]

global-min-publish-age = "3 days"

On Hacker News, developer woodruffw argued cooldowns need to coexist with immediate security patching:

You should do both: you should let normal updates cool down,

and

you should immediately patch security advisories.

One of the biggest ergonomic problems with cooldowns is that many tools let the former goal obstruct the latter. Both should be part of the state machine of resolution itself, rather than things that get layered on.

ImportStatic found on the beta that cargo install ignores the setting entirely and that an update could even downgrade a forced security fix, something the release notes also flag as a known caveat. The approach sits alongside GitHub's Dependabot cooldown protection but builds the age check into dependency resolution itself.

Other notable additions include core::mem::DropGuard for running a closure on every exit path, std::mem::conjure_zst for zero-sized types in unsafe code, plus smaller ergonomic wins such as bool::toggle, str::trim_prefix, str::trim_suffix and Box::map.

Upgrading uses rustup update stable; Rust 1.99 is no longer supported, and 1.101 follows the six-week cadence around 24 December 2026.

Rust is an open-source systems programming language maintained by the Rust Foundation and a global community, designed to empower developers to build reliable and efficient software through strong type safety, memory safety guarantees without a garbage collector, and a mature package ecosystem through Cargo.

item.description:

AWS recently doubled the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes. The new limit applies to synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping invocations in all commercial regions, at standard pricing and without an opt-in. The 15-minute ceiling had stood since 2018, after 60 seconds at launch in 2014 and five minutes from 2015.

Raising the limit is a configuration change per function, and Lambda rejects any value above 1,800 seconds with a validation error:

aws lambda update-function-configuration \

--function-name my-demo-function \

--timeout 1800

The change covers one of the three shapes Lambda took this year. Web Functions keep 15 minutes, and Lambda MicroVMs allow eight hours, while on Lambda Managed Instances synchronous invocations now get 30 minutes and asynchronous ones keep the 90 minutes introduced in September. AWS names agentic AI requests that chain model and tool calls, media transcoding, Monte Carlo simulations, and report generation as the workloads that outgrew 15 minutes.

According to Tarun Rai Madan, Dan Slusariuc, and Snehil Ameta, the authors of the announcement, the first thing to check before raising the timeout is capacity:

Concurrency equals requests per second multiplied by average duration in seconds. At the same request rate, a function that runs for 30 minutes instead of 15 needs twice the concurrency. For example, 1 request per second at 30 minutes each needs 1,800 concurrent executions.

The rest of the post is about what sits around the function. An SQS queue's visibility timeout has to be at least six times the function timeout, which means three hours. Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams read one batch per shard at a time, so a slow function slows the shard. Amazon MQ, DocumentDB and Kafka mappings created before November 19 stay at 14 minutes. A NAT gateway still drops idle connections after 350 seconds, and the Init phase keeps its 10-second limit.

Wibo van der Sluis, an independent AWS practitioner, tested the SQS rule in eu-west-1 by raising a function to 1,800 seconds behind a queue with a 90-minute visibility timeout and then lowering the queue to 60 seconds. Both changes were accepted with the mapping still enabled, while a new mapping from the same queue was refused:

So the check exists, but only at creation. One more thing the test showed: at creation, Lambda compared the queue with the function timeout itself, not with six times it. I did not test where exactly that line sits, so treat the six times as guidance you enforce yourself.

He adds that an asynchronous function which times out three times has run for 90 minutes before the event reaches a dead-letter queue, and concludes that 30 minutes is the wrong fix for slow code behind an API.

Luc van Donkersgoed, principal engineer at NS and AWS Serverless Hero, writes:

Hell froze over. AWS Lambda now supports 30-minute timeouts. I am not sure how I feel about this.

The comments under the post took two directions. Magnus Eriksson, architect and former AWS employee, notes that Lambda "is anyhow quite expensive per CPU second compared to EC2" and would still reserve it for short-lived spiky loads. Matthew Bonig, AWS DevTools Hero and co-author of The CDK Book, looked further ahead: "Eventually it'll be 8 hours, and then nobody will be able to understand when to use it vs. MicroVMs."

On Reddit, the most-upvoted reply welcomed the change because it avoids Fargate and ECS for hour-long batch jobs. The answer under it was that Fargate is beautifully simple. One commenter sets out where the longer limit fits:

A 30 minute run still bills for the full duration at your configured memory, so check the cost per invocation before moving batch style work here, and keep the handler idempotent with a dead letter queue, because a failure or timeout partway through a long run can leave partial work behind. For multi step work, long running jobs, or anything that needs clear state and retries, Step Functions with Fargate or ECS is still usually cleaner.

Joseph Emison, CTO of Branch Insurance, reads the move as Lambda team recognizing that Cloud Run is its most compelling competitor. Cloud Run services allow 60 minutes per request, and Azure Functions on the Flex Consumption and Premium plans enforce no maximum, with a 60-minute grace period during scale-in. AWS has not said whether the Lambda limit will move again.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mouli Mukherjee, Engineering Manager for Data Infrastructure at OpenAI, argued that AI agents are most useful not for rebuilding a data platform, but for the open-ended operational work that is hard to turn into fixed playbooks. OpenAI’s platform runs at exabyte scale, with hundreds of thousands of datasets and a Spark fleet on millions of cores, and Mukherjee showed how Codex-driven agents can take on that kind of work when the right systems sit underneath them.

Mukherjee clearly distinguished between deterministic systems and agents. She stated that anything requiring consistent outputs for the same inputs, such as access control, configuration resolution, and data correctness guarantees, should remain within the realm of proper systems. Agents utilize these systems as tools and do not attempt to reimplement them. As she expressed:

We should definitely build the systems where we want guarantees and guardrails.

Agents earn their place where failure modes and remediations cannot be fully enumerated in advance, such as debugging: follow the evidence, decide what to try next, and stay inside the tools’ guarantees.

The Spark upgrade outlines steps taken to ensure safety. The team first built a shadow-run service for testing, which reused production inputs and operated on a low-priority queue to avoid impacting live operations. They also implemented a configuration override service to prevent experiments from changing global settings and developed a validation skill to compare production and shadow runs. After these safeguards were in place, agents claimed jobs, launched shadow runs, reviewed validation reports, classified errors, and transitioned jobs to the new Spark version.

Mukherjee reported that the same primitives now cover more of routine platform operations. Agents can tune job efficiency continuously by inspecting query plans, trying a config change, comparing runs, and iterating. For lower-risk incremental library releases, the team sometimes skips the shadow step and promotes directly, trading capacity for higher rollback risk. Jobs that pass shadow validation but later fail in production can auto-roll back to the previous Spark version so pipelines keep running without manual intervention. On the support side, agents can search past incident reports, suggest runbook updates, trace why a table is stale through orchestrator and scheduler logs, and help users understand access-control denials, while permissions still enforce the user’s own credentials.

Mukherjee recommended starting with the repetitive, open-ended tasks where judgment matters and failure modes are too numerous to hard-code, building the safety mechanisms first, and only then letting agents operate inside those bounds so experimentation stays repeatable, observable, and reversible.

Few corporate rivalries are as fierce as the one between Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The world’s leading manufacturer of memory chips and the world’s leading manufacturer of high-bandwidth memory, respectively, are fighting for the title of South Korea’s most valuable company. In one area, though, the two are on the same team: Both back Rebellions, the $2.3 billion chip startup cofounded by Sunghyun Park—a veteran of Intel, SpaceX, and Morgan Stanley—that fronts South Korea’s push for sovereign silicon or AI chips that don’t depend on market leader Nvidia or any other U.S. or Chinese company.

Park’s company sits at the center of government policy. “AI requires huge capital and huge talent,” he says. “Instead of having multiple players compete, the Korean government said, ‘We need one champion. SK Hynix, please help him. Samsung, please help him. SK Telecom, KT’—top two data center companies—‘please become Rebellions’ customers.’”

Rebellions may be the clearest test of whether sovereign AI can produce something more than an expensive also-ran. Korea is funneling its best resources toward Rebellions: Samsung’s foundries, SK Hynix’s memory, and government money. The Korea National Growth Fund co-led Rebellions’ $400 million round in March.

Will it pay off? Rebellions eventually wants public investors to back a risky bet on a chip startup in a market that—for now—is skeptical of AI stocks. Still, Park is hopeful. Rebellions’ backers make it “more powerful compared to any other player in the United States,” he says. But market volatility and a wave of shelved data center IPOs will put his confidence to the test.

Park took the long road to national-champion-in-waiting. A graduate of the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, he spent his compulsory military service in Afghanistan alongside the U.S. Army, where he learned English. Afterward, he earned a PhD in electrical engineering and computer science at MIT, and worked in chip engineering roles at Intel, SpaceX, and Morgan Stanley in the U.S. before returning to Korea to launch Rebellions.

Park and his cofounders—including Jinwook Oh, who designed AI chips at IBM, and Hyo-eun Kim, who developed deep-learning technology at a medical AI startup—founded Rebellions in 2020. It’s a “fabless” chip startup in that it handles only design and contracts manufacturing (or “fabrication”) out to a third party—in this case, Samsung.

In 2024, Rebellions merged with Sapeon, another chip designer backed by the SK Group. Samsung invested in the combined company in 2025.

Rebellions is part of a wave of startups challenging Nvidia by going after inference—what happens when someone uses ChatGPT, Claude, or DeepSeek—rather than training, which builds the models.

Inference is “highly cost-sensitive,” says Rakesh Kumar, a University of Illinois engineering professor and author of The Chip Age: How Semiconductors Became the World’s Most Powerful Resource. A $2 difference in price could be the reason someone chooses OpenAI over Anthropic.

Park, too, is pitching efficiency, rather than pure power. “From the hardware side, we claim only one metric,” he says. “Tokens per second, per dollar, per watt.”

Outside the U.S. and China—the clear leaders in the AI race—countries are trying to figure out how they can insulate themselves from the whims of foreign suppliers and governments.

South Korea may take the idea most seriously. It has run a state-backed Korean-language-model competition since June 2025, and its “AI for All” initiative plans to give Koreans free local chatbots. Stanford’s Institute for Human-Centered AI counts only three countries with more than a handful of “notable AI models”: the U.S., with 59; China, with 35; and South Korea, with eight.

“Even my mom talks about sovereign AI, [and] she doesn’t know what sovereign AI is,” Park says.

The catch is that sovereign AI programs may lead to models and chips that are less capable, less efficient, and more costly than what comes out of the U.S. or China. Such startups can’t take advantage of the same economies of scale as established players and are selling their products to a smaller customer base. “You’re spending all this money with no guarantee of success,” Kumar says. Without Nvidia’s scale, “you might actually have higher costs.”

Rebellions, which counts backers KT and SK Telecom as customers, hopes to list in Seoul next year, though Park says it will depend on market conditions. The government wants a Korean listing first—for “national security”—before a second listing abroad, he says.

Other AI IPOs have gone astray. At least three AI-related companies—Australia’s Firmus and AirTrunk, and SK Hynix’s U.S. unit Solidigm—suspended their IPOs in October, citing market uncertainty. Investors have also punished AI shares amid worries about high debt and massive capital expenditure.

Park is unfazed by market swings—perhaps a benefit of having the Korean government and the country’s two most valuable companies as backers. But he knows that AI firms will eventually have to prove they can turn a profit. He expects the judgment to come by 2029: “Then, the market will test whether these investments are paying off or not.”

What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?

Energy bills are to soar in January, as prices governed by regulator Ofgem's cap rise at the coldest time of the year.

The cap affects millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales, and reflects higher wholesale gas costs which have been pushed up by the US-Israel war with Iran.

It means people on variable tariffs should give an accurate meter reading, ensure they are receiving all the support to which they are entitled, and take care over energy use.

What is the energy cap and how is it changing?

The energy cap fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used.

It covers more than 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by the regulator Ofgem every three months, external.

It affects those paying by direct debit, by standard credit (they pay when they get a bill), or prepayment meters in slightly different ways.

Most of the increase in the energy price cap has, and will be, driven by higher gas prices.

The government's decision to temporarily remove VAT from domestic electricity bills has cut about Â£45 a year from a typical bill.

Meanwhile, millions of households will receive a Â£100 automatic payment to help cover winter costs.

The typical annual usage figure applies to the first category: dual-fuel households on a standard variable tariff which pay by direct debit.

But customers' actual bills depend on the amount of energy used and how they pay for it.

The roughly 11 million households on fixed tariffs do not see their prices change until the end of their fixed term.

Ofgem regulates the energy market in England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has a separate system.

What is a typical household?

Although the price cap sets the unit prices for gas and electricity, your household's actual bill depends on the overall amount of energy you use, and how you pay for it.

Where you live, the type of property you have, how energy efficient it is, how many people live there, and the weather all make a difference.

The Ofgem cap is illustrated using "typical" household energy use in a year with a single bill for gas and electricity settled by direct debit.

The vast majority of people pay their bill this way to help spread payments across the year.

In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back due to high prices in recent years while energy efficiency has improved.

Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.

Should I take a meter reading when the energy cap changes?

Submitting a meter reading when the cap changes means you are not charged for estimated usage at the wrong rate.

This is especially important when prices go up.

Customers with working smart meters do not need to submit a reading as their bill is calculated automatically.

What are standing charges and how are they changing?

Ofgem also controls standing charges, which are a fixed daily fee to cover the costs of connecting households to gas and electricity supplies. These vary slightly by region, external and payment method.

Between 1 October and 31 December 2026, average standing charges for direct debit customers will be 54.83p a day for electricity and 29.68p a day for gas.

The electricity charge is lower than the amount charged in the previous three-month period, while the gas charge is largely unchanged.

Campaigners have long argued that standing charges are unfair because they make up a bigger proportion of the bill for low-energy households. Others say it just shifts the cost from one part of the bill to another rather than cutting it.

The government has announced plans to remove gas standing charges, although no details have been published on how that will happen

Should I fix my energy prices?

Fixed deals provide certainty for a set period â often a year, or longer â but if energy prices drop while you are on the deal, you could be stuck at a higher price.

You may also have to pay a penalty to leave a fixed deal early if you change your mind.

Experts recommend checking whole-of-market energy price comparison sites to help find the best deal and studying the details of exit fees.

What else has changed about the way energy bills are calculated?

Since 1 April, energy bill charges related to the low-income household insulation scheme - called the Energy Company Obligation - have been scrapped, and for three years, renewable energy projects will be 75%-funded by general taxation instead of a levy on energy bills.

Nearly everyone in England, Wales and Scotland will benefit from this cut, although the amounts will vary between households.

However, the cost of maintaining and strengthening energy network infrastructure like power lines, cables and gas pipes is rising.

Customers will pay part of the cost of the upgrade, through an additional Â£108 added to energy bills by 2031.

'We've turned the heating down by 2.5C'

item.title: Why more Americans are choosing to pay over time
item.description:

Why it is here: Analysis of a payment trend with useful vocabulary and context.

Paying with a credit card for lunch is routine today. It wasn’t always so. In a 1993 television report covering Burger King’s trial acceptance of credit cards, one customer objected, saying, “I think it’s pretty bad if you have to use a credit card when you go to a fast food restaurant. For something as little as $3.10.” Her objection assumed using credit for a small purchase meant you could not afford it. Newer payment tools face that same assumption today, even though the ways people manage everyday spending have changed.

Today we see a major shift in how people across income levels access wages they have already earned and use deferred-payment options instead of traditional financing like credit cards. Block recently surveyed deferred-payment users, finding that 49% used cash advances or early wage access in the past year, alongside growing adoption of buy now, pay later. Survey findings also show about two in five Afterpay Pay in 4 and Pay Monthly users reported household incomes of $100,000 or more, underscoring that these tools reach across income brackets rather than serving only people without other options.

The common thread behind both habits is timing. People often have money on the way that has not hit their account yet, and they use these tools to line up an expense with an incoming paycheck. By our estimate, U.S. workers at any given time have earned about $260 billion in wages they have not yet been paid. Among surveyed deferred-payment users, 65% financed an expense at least once in the past year because money was coming from a paycheck, refund, or another source, but had not arrived yet.

That timing helps explain why many consumers are moving away from revolving card balances. Federal Reserve survey data shows the same share of credit cardholders who carried a balance at some point in the year fell from 57% to 45% over the past decade. Over a shorter span, adult use of buy now, pay later rose from 10% in 2021 to 16% in 2025, according to the Federal Reserve. When carrying a card balance is costly, a plan with a defined cost and payoff date can become more attractive.

When we ask customers what they want from a payment plan, predictability wins. In our study, 57% preferred a fixed payment schedule with the same amount, the same date and a clear endpoint over payment flexibility. One customer in our research put it plainly, saying, “We could probably buy this upfront, but then we’d be talking about a cushion of 200, 300 dollars at the end of October, which is probably cutting it too close.” Spreading payments lets households protect a cash buffer instead of draining their account at once.

In many situations, these products provide consumers a lifeline, but at other times, they simply provide choice. In the same study, 53% of respondents’ most recent financed transactions were necessity-driven, where available funds could not cover the expense when needed, while 47% were ones the customer could have paid upfront. Those numbers describe different situations, not different types of people. The same customer can use a payment plan out of necessity one month and to preserve savings the next.

Importantly, these consumers are building a habit of repayment, but traditional credit files miss so much of this picture. Legacy scoring models look backward at reported debt, treating a thin borrowing history as a lack of creditworthiness even when someone earns steady income and pays bills on time. Our underwriting models consider current cash flow, historical cash flow trends, and a customer’s debt history. By weighing the frequency and stability of incoming deposits against recurring commitments, we can spot repayment capacity a static credit report overlooks. That ongoing view also lets us reduce a limit when incoming cash slows, keeping commitments aligned with what a customer can handle.

For credit to fit how money actually moves, regulation has to keep pace with how these products work. Policymakers should support the responsible use of cash-flow data in underwriting so capable borrowers are not shut out for lacking a traditional credit file. Regulators should also judge financial products by what they actually do, including loan size, duration, cost and repayment structure, rather than forcing them into roles built for older categories. Clear disclosures should state the total dollar cost, payment due dates, when repayment ends and what happens if a payment is missed so every customer knows the full commitment before they agree.

The Defense Department will detonate the material in a controlled blast at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, about 10 miles from the Illinois border. Although the goal is to eliminate the risk of an accidental explosion, the detonation carries another threat: a plume of lead-laden dust that could settle over homes and farmland for miles around.

Here’s what to know about this unusual operation and the risk it poses.

Why is the army detonating old munitions?

Army inspectors discovered in March that 68 drums of decades-old lead azide had begun to crystallize, making it increasingly sensitive to friction, vibration, and temperature changes. Even the slightest movement could trigger an explosion.

“The lead azide has aged. It’s become unstable to the point where moving it or even allowing it to sit, on the odd chance that it receives some sort of shock or friction, could lead to a spontaneous explosion,” said Greg Domski, associate provost and professor of chemistry and biochemistry at Augustana College in Rock Island, Illinois.

After consulting with the Environmental Protection Agency, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms, and other agencies, the Army decided the best option was to detonate the material where it sits. The plan to do so has been ongoing in the months since.

What is lead azide?

Lead azide is a compound of lead and nitrogen, commonly used in detonators to set off other explosives. About 9,700 pounds of the material will be detonated.

While the Army has destroyed weapons and materials in the past, it has never destroyed so large an amount of lead azide. This operation requires detonating 9,700 pounds of the material stored in 68 drums.

“We detonate all the time, but we have not detonated lead azide at this quantity,” said Lori McFate, public affairs specialist with the Army Sustainment Command in Bettendorf, Iowa.

The Army delayed the operation after elected officials in both states raised concerns about safety. Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds and Governor-elect Rob Sand were joined by other politicians in calling for a delay. The environmental organization Earthjustice also sued to try to pause the detonation.

Where will the plume go?

Current forecasts based on U.S. Army modeling show the plume traveling southwest away from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. The modeling for the canceled November 20 detonation had the plume crossing the Mississippi River and reaching as far as Illinois.

- Double exposure to wildfire air pollution and heatwaves on the same days has become more common globally, according to a 20-year study by Monash University scientists.

- An average of 916 million people were exposed to a day of wildfire haze and heatwaves in two decades, more than half of the global population.

- The top five countries worst affected were the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, Mexico, Brazil and Russia.

- Indonesia led with the highest annual average number of people affected, reaching 101 million per year in 2010-2019.

JAKARTA — While the worst of Indonesia’s wildfire and haze season for 2026 may be over with fewer hotspots detected in recent weeks, this wasn’t the only hazard faced by residents in the months-long crisis.

Take, for example, Palangka Raya in Central Kalimantan province, one of the areas worst affected by this year’s wildfires in the country. From August to October 2026, fine-particle pollution in the provincial capital averaged nearly 10 times the 2021 to 2025 level, according to data from Indonesia’s meteorological agency, BMKG. Meanwhile, as haze choked the city in August, its residents also experienced a heatwave, according to data from BMKG.

Exposure to wildfire air pollution and heatwaves on the same days has become more common globally, according to a new study published in the journal Science Advances.

Researchers from Monash University, in Melbourne, Australia, analyzed 20 years of data, from 2000 to 2019, and found that, on average, 916 million people, or 56% of the global population, experienced one co-exposure day annually.

The total number of people increased by 287 million from one decade to the next, according to the study. The top five countries worst affected were the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, Mexico, Brazil and Russia.

The study blamed the double exposure on climate change, saying it “has increased the frequency and intensity of concurrent heatwaves and landscape fire events, resulting in more profound impacts.”

Indonesia had the highest annual average number of people affected, reaching 101 million per year in 2010-2019, up from 72 million in the previous decade.

Wu Yao, one of the study’s authors and adjunct research fellow at the School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine at Monash University, Melbourne, said the increase in Indonesia was driven mainly by people experiencing the two hazards more frequently, rather than by population growth.

The analysis showed that in Indonesia, approximately 82% of the increase in total co-exposure was attributable to changes in exposure frequency, while population changes accounted for only about 18%, Wu told Mongabay via email.

Moreover, the average number of heatwave exposure days per person per year in Indonesia had more than doubled, from approximately 17 days in 2000-2009 to 42 days in 2010-2019, Wu added. Meanwhile, wildfire smoke exposure days rose slightly, from about 27 to 28 days.

“This suggests that the increasing frequency of heatwaves may have been an important contributor to the rise in co-exposure, making people more likely to experience extreme heat when wildfire smoke pollution occurs,” Wu told Mongabay.

Co-exposure risks are not evenly distributed across Indonesia. Wu said southern Sumatra and central and southern Kalimantan experienced the combined hazards most frequently, with particularly notable increases in eastern Kalimantan. All of these areas have been prone to recurring wildfires and haze in past decades, including during El Niño in 2026.

Java, Indonesia’s most populated island, had also “experienced a substantial population exposure burden,” she said. Wu added that co-exposure there did not rise steadily but fluctuated from year to year, with particularly high levels in 2015 and 2019 — both El Niño years.

The researchers did note that El Niño can influence heatwave trends in Southeast Asia and Australia. However, the study did not examine the influence of El Niño, peatland conditions or land use on Indonesia’s exposure patterns, Wu said, so it could not identify what drove the changes in particular locations.

Indonesia is not the only Southeast Asian country badly affected. Cambodia, which experienced the highest fire density in the region in 2019–2020, saw one of the sharpest co-exposure increases globally, climbing from 40th place in 2000–2009 to ninth in 2010–2019 for co-exposure days per person. The number of average co-exposure days per year rose from about 1.6 to 12.1, according to the study.

Toll on public health

The study was released in October, when Indonesia was battling wildfires, said to be the worst in 11 years. From January to Oct. 31, 2025, around 65,900 hot spots had been detected — a figure second only to the approximately 85,600 hot spots logged in the same period in 2015, according to data BMKG shared with Mongabay.

An independent assessment by The TreeMap, published on Nusantara Atlas, estimates that around 1.9 million hectares (4.7 million acres) of land across Indonesia were affected by fire between January and September 2026, 38% higher than its estimate for the same period in 2019.

The 2026 haze crisis in Indonesia has taken a heavy toll on public health, affecting at least 40 million people in the country. The Health Ministry recorded 333,470 acute respiratory infection (ARI) cases between Aug. 18 and Oct. 21 in seven Sumatra and Kalimantan provinces worst affected by wildfires.

According to the nonprofit Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), short-term exposure to fine-particle pollution from Indonesia’s wildfires contributed to an estimated 5,200 deaths in August and September in the country.

The haze also traveled across the border, affecting millions more in Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines and Timor-Leste, forcing school closures and causing increases in upper respiratory tract infection, asthma and conjunctivitis cases.

Reaching 100 animals is hardly a guarantee of survival, since many of the recovered species still require intensive management.

Among species that recovered after direct intervention, the median time to reach 100 individuals was 18 years.

Australia’s Lord Howe woodhen (Hypotaenidia sylvestris) had dwindled to just 23 birds by the late 1970s.

Conservationists removed feral pigs and cats, and bred the birds in captivity and released them. The population hovered around 200 for decades. After rats were eradicated in 2019, it climbed to 1,638 by 2024.

Majority-owned by China’s Tsingshan Holding Group and home to more than 50 companies and more than 100,000 workers, the industrial park, known as IMIP, processes nickel into stainless steel and the basic materials that go into making batteries for electric vehicles and storage for solar and other intermittent sources of renewable energy.

It may also be among Indonesia’s most dangerous industrial places to work. How dangerous, though, is a matter of debate.

Unions, representing about 10,000 workers, including those in IMIP smelters, have said they won’t sign on to a collective bargaining agreement, or CBA, in part because employers won’t allow them to participate on health and safety committees that file formal incident reports.

The issue has been a live one since December 2023, when a deadly blast at a nickel smelter furnace owned by Indonesia Tsingshan Stainless Steel, a Tsingshan subsidiary, ultimately claimed the lives of 21 workers.

On Nov. 7 this year, unions, including the Federation of Independent Industrial Workers’ Unions (FSPIM), the Indonesian Morowali Industrial Labor Union (SBIMI), and the Mining and Energy Industry Labor Unions (SBIPE), called off a five day sit-in at government labor department offices in Morowali district, Central Sulawesi province. The sit-in had been launched in a bid, union leaders say, to forestall efforts on the part of employers to file the agreement with the government, which would have brought it into force.

Workers have been without a new collective agreement since 2023. The Morowali labor department extended until this month the two-year contract expiring in November 2025, after talks to replace it collapsed. Union members say employers had failed to attend crucial talks that included membership on health and safety committees.

“We want to avoid the same situation from last year when their employers just used the old CBA from the year before,” Zainal Arfin, advocacy coordinator and FSPIM delegate at the CBA talks, told Mongabay.

During the talks, companies also demanded workers report for their shifts one hour before they start and rejected demands for mandatory breaks after at least four hours, Zainal said. Efforts to reach a spokesperson for IMIP for comment were unsuccessful.

“This collective bargaining agreement serves as a foundational instrument for establishing worker welfare,” Komang Jordi, the FSPIM chair, told Mongabay in an interview.

“It is perfectly legitimate for workers to reject it if they believe it does not serve the interests of the working class.”

Thirty-nine workers, including Indonesian and Chinese nationals, have died in the IMIP area from workplace accidents during the seven years to 2023, when employment at the industrial park surged roughly tenfold to 74,000 people, according to government data.

But what counts as a workplace fatality is at issue. One example: back-to-back accidents at PT Dexin Steel Indonesia (DSI), a steelmaker operating in the industrial park, in October 2024.

An explosion and fire killed an Indonesian crane worker, prompting IMIP to issue a public statement. The following day, a Chinese national working on repairs at the same site was reportedly taken to hospital for severe dehydration, and later died. There has been no public statement from the company or government officials on the latter incident.

Limited time and resources to verify incidents that occur in remote places, plus an often distracted public, mean many accidents go unnoticed, Li Qiang, executive director of China Labor Watch, told Mongabay in a written message. China Labor Watch first reported the fatality of the Chinese national at DSI.

“We sometimes share information about these incidents with journalists, but news outlets are not always interested in reporting them,” Li said.

“As a result, the accidents that become public may represent only a small portion of those that actually occur.”

There were a total of 107 fatalities at nickel processing sites during the six years to 2025, according to a media report citing labor ministry inspector Hugo Nainggolan. Hugo, who is also a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Indonesia, painted a picture of a culture among nickel processors of targets first, safety second.

The companies “work in a way where all that matters is that their targets keep moving,” Hugo is quoted as saying.

To be sure, the dissenting unions that are balking at the new agreement are in the minority. Ten have lined up in favor, including the Metal, Machinery, and Electronics Federation under the Confederation of All-Indonesia Workers’ Union (KSBSI).

“We hope that there is a path toward reaching an agreement so that we don’t stagnate with the last CBA,” Bernard Rolensius Siahaan, secretary of the federation’s Morowali branch, said in a statement.…

How to make cider at home: simple step-by-step guide

Cider expert Gabe Cook gives a beginner's guide to making homemade cider, including tips on selecting apples, extraction and fermentation

Making cider at home is simpler than it sounds – here’s a clear step-by-step method using fresh apples, plus what to expect as it ferments.

Why make your own cider at home?

As well as it being a great way to use up surplus fruit, if you have an apple tree in your garden, homemade cider is a straightforward and affordable drink to make once you've got the equipment and the hang of the process.

Do I need a press to make cider?

A fruit press is the easiest and most effective way to extract juice from the apples, and these can be bought online for a range of prices, starting at around £50. You can also use a juicer or squeeze the apple pulp by hand but this is a lot more labour-intensive and will yield smaller volumes of cider.

Many people have an apple tree in their garden. It may be one that they have planted themselves for ornamental purposes or an older tree of an unknown variety. But how often is the fruit of this tree actually put to good use?

Sometimes the incentive isn’t there, especially if the apples are too bitter to eat. But with often hectic lives and schedules the fruit simply rots on the ground before we have a chance to harvest and enjoy it.

Cider-making is essentially an easy process and a great way to prevent that food waste. Find ways to cook with cider in our useful guide, then check out other drinks guides, including how to make mead or our recipes for homemade kefir and kombucha.

You just need a few simple pieces of equipment to turn a wealth of unwanted apples into their ultimate form: glorious cider.

How to make your own cider

What you will need to make cider from scratch

- Clean and washed apples

- Apple mill, food processor or strong pole with a wide bucket

- Basket press

- Straining cloth

- Demijohn or plastic container with lid and airlock which can be used as a fermentation vessel

- Clean plastic container for fermented liquid

- Hydrometer

- Cultured yeast

- Sulphur dioxide (usually in form of Campden tablets)

- Beer bottles for cider storage

A fantastic range of milling and pressing equipment for all scales and types of hobbyist can be found at vigopresses.co.uk.

If you're looking to upgrade your kitchen kit, here are some recommendations that might come in handy for making cider.

Step 1: select the apples

Any apple can be used for making cider but it must be accepted that nature will determine what the flavour profile will end up like.

To make the best cider you need to ensure that the fruit is ripe. This can be done with a simple prod test – when you can leave an indentation in the skin with your thumbnail, they’re ready to go. Bruised apples are fine but avoid any that are mouldy as they can spoil the batch.

Importantly the fruit needs to be clean so as to not introduce bacteria. You don’t want any mud or bird poo, so wash your apples with a hose pipe or by dunking them into a bucket of water.

Step 2: juice extraction

This step of the home cider-making process is probably the most challenging because of the need for some equipment and/or elbow grease.

There are three options to extract the apple juice:

- Use an apple mill – a contraption designed to crush, chop or chew the apples into a pulp.

- Pop halved apples into a food processor, using the coarsest blade, if wanting a smaller quantity of cider.

- Put the apples into a bucket, known as a 'trub', and pound them with a big pole until they turn into a pulp.

Prior to use the equipment does not need to sterilised but it should be thoroughly rinsed.

Regardless of your methodology this pulp now needs to be squeezed or pressed in order to separate juice from the solid component, which is not wanted. This is done by applying pressure to the pulp and straining the juice through a suitable medium.

The most basic form of kit for this part of the process is a basket press, which you can buy fairly cheaply and easily. If you’re looking to make hundreds rather than tens of litres, a small pack press would be best.

No matter what press type, the premise is the same: to exert pressure. The squeezed pulp releases the juice, which passes through a cloth, ensuring a most satisfying flow of juice which can be collected in a bucket or jug.

Step 3: fermentation and maturation

First, choose a fermenting vessel. If you are making a small quantity, a 4.5-litre demijohn is ideal.

For a larger quantity, you may wish to use a 25-litre plastic container. When you use a basket press, you would hope to achieve a 50% juice yield: that is to say that every 10kg of fruit pulped and pressed will equate to 5 litres (9 pints) of juice.

Ensure your container is free of detritus and thoroughly rinsed before pouring in your juice. If you are concerned your container is still not clean, you could use a basic sanitiser for a belt-and-braces approach.

You may choose to measure the sugar content of the juice using a hydrometer – it looks like a thermometer with a bulbous end. Put this into the juice, it bobs around and you read a measurement of where the hydrometer sits in the juice. It's actually measuring the density of the juice which is a proxy for the sugar content, which you can then extrapolate into a potential alcohol.

How to Use a Fork for Even Cheese Slices

Rather than eyeballing the thickness of each slice, you can use the evenly spaced tines of a fork to mark the cheese beforehand, giving yourself a cutting guide.

Start with a wedge of cheese and gently press the tips of the fork’s tines into the face you’ll be cutting into, leaving a row of small, evenly spaced indentations. Repeat as needed across the back of the wedge, then use a sharp knife to slice between the marks. Having those little reference points makes it much easier to maintain a consistent thickness from one slice to the next.

Is It Rude to Bring Your Own Food to Thanksgiving?

Thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year. Do you serve canned cranberry sauce or get fresh cranberries to make one from scratch? Should sweet potatoes be combined with marshmallows? And what time are we eating dinner?

For the record, I say serve both kinds of cranberry sauce, get marshmallows off my sweet potatoes and we eat dinner whenever the host says dinner is ready. I can already feel the consternation boiling up if you disagree. But that is all part of the magic of the holiday!

I think it’s beautiful that no two families celebrate Thanksgiving the same way. Although, with all that preparation and planning, emotions can run high. It is very difficult to cook for large groups of people, and even more so when people have strong opinions about the meal. So if a guest brings their own food, is that considerate or rude? Should they bring enough to share or just what they want to eat?

As a food writer and frequent host, I am going to tell you how to navigate this etiquette dilemma.

Is it OK to bring your own food to Thanksgiving dinner?

Once upon a time, a member of my extended family brought KFC to my house because he did not like what my mom was cooking for dinner. This is undoubtedly rude and totally not OK. But it’s also a more extreme example of what people think of when they imagine “bringing your own food” somewhere.

The short answer here is: no, it’s not OK to bring your own food to Thanksgiving dinner unless it has specifically been identified as a potluck-style meal. You can—and should!—ask the host if you can bring something, but if they say no, you need to respect that.

A more realistic answer is probably it depends. I know, that’s kind of annoying. But I think this is a really nuanced question, and I want to do it justice. There really isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. Here are some scenarios:

This host is a terrible cook

I’m sorry to break it to you, but this isn’t a real reason. It’s definitely a bummer, but sometimes that’s just how things go. Make some light-hearted jokes about it in the group chat with your cousins, and suck it up. This is one meal on one day, and it is not a good enough reason to bring your own food. Have a big breakfast before heading over, and take very small portions. If anyone notices, a simple “I’m saving room for dessert” is a perfect get-out-of-jail-free card.

There is never enough food

I suggest bringing appetizers or snacks instead of something for the main meal. Snacks are often overlooked when there is already a turkey in the oven and a pot on every burner. Tell the host you’re bringing a veggie tray and some chips and dips to snack on before the meal. Plus, it’s a separate thing and doesn’t really step on the host’s toes the way bringing an entire lasagna would.

You don’t like Thanksgiving food

First, know that I support you. But second, this is a you problem, and I think you know that. Load up on dinner rolls and volunteer to make a pot of coffee and do the dishes after the meal. It doesn’t have to be a big deal, and you can get back to regular food on Friday.

Can you bring your own food to Thanksgiving if you have allergies?

This is the biggest exception and one that merits its own section. If you or members of your immediate family have food allergies, you can absolutely bring your own food—but it’s really important to coordinate with the host. It shouldn’t feel like an ambush. Communicating to the host that you will be bringing gluten-free rolls or a dairy-free macaroni and cheese to ensure that you have something safe to eat is totally fine.

And I would argue that this is more relevant with kids than adults. It’s really important for kids to feel welcome in your home and to enjoy this holiday safely with all their family members. Anything you can do to alleviate stress or anxiety is not only good manners but also totally in the spirit of Thanksgiving.

A Final Note

It’s good guest etiquette to communicate with the host in advance. Once you receive the invite, volunteer to bring something. If you’re a champion baker, offer to make the pies or a nice, crusty sourdough loaf. You can even say you have a great Brussels sprouts recipe that’s been a hit with the family lately and you’d love to share it with more people. Or, simply ask if they would prefer a bottle of red or white wine.

Thanksgiving might be the most food-centric day of the year. But in my experience, the food becomes secondary as I sit around the table talking and laughing with my loved ones. There is always a moment where the stress melts away and I’m filled with an overwhelming sense of joy and gratitude. And that, my friends, is what the holiday is all about.

Assemble covers miniature agricultural buildings in intense blue pigment for Building Blue exhibition in Tokyo

Architecture collective Assemble has created small, climbable cedar buildings that “play with scale” to showcase a new pigment made from industrial waste at Tokyo‘s SKAC gallery.

With the exhibition, the UK-based collective said it aimed to “explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour”.

The architects are using the Building Blue exhibition to showcase a new pigment, made by design studio Matter at hand for Assemble from local waste material. It will also be used in Assemble’s Play Earth Park – a campsite under development in rural Japan.

“The pigment was essentially created by analysing local material waste streams in Toyama and exploring what kind of different colours could be produced from them,” Assemble co-founder Maria Lisogorskaya told Dezeen.

“In the end, the blue uses a combination of rice husk ash, limestone filter dust, recycled glass and copper, which are mixed together with water to form a thick clay-like paste and then heated in an electric kiln to around 950ºC,” she continued.

“The materials react to form a new crystal phase – known as cuprorivaite, which is bright blue.”

To show it off, the designers constructed numerous miniature houses from Japanese cedar that draw on the agricultural buildings found close to where the pigment material was sourced.

“The form of the structures plays with the agricultural buildings within the dispersed settlement of rural Toyama; these buildings evolve over time, adapting to what’s needed, often evolving interesting geometries,” Assemble co-founder Lewis Jones told Dezeen.

“We tried to play with scale and make the buildings surreal, creating miniature versions of them for play.”

The buildings have deliberately simple yet evocative geometries that nod to the structures that inspired them. Among them is a barn-like building surrounded by hay bales.

Assemble’s aim was for visitors to be able to climb and explore the structures.

“We hope that the buildings are climbed on and inhabited; and this exhibition is the beginning of the structures’ life as a play space outside SKWAT,” Lisogorskaya said.

“The spirit of resourcefulness, fun, and reimagining of our environments is at the core of the project and we look forward to seeing how the structures are used in ways we didn’t expect.”

The exhibition, which also showcases raw materials used to create the blue colour and products covered in it, is on show in Skwat Kameari Art Centre (SKAC’s) Park gallery in Kameari, Tokyo.

Assemble said it chose to showcase it here as it feels the gallery has a similar spirit to its own UK bases.

“We think SKAC is an amazing interdisciplinary space, and its spirit resonates with how we have set up our studios and labs in London and Liverpool,” Jones said.

“Bringing together design, material experimentation with other arts practices as a more satisfying and richer way of being in the city,” he continued.

SKAC recently opened two new gallery spaces, Material Matters (MM) and Space III, as part of a major extension.

The east Tokyo gallery has previously shown exhibitions including anime-informed chairs by Kwangho Lee and reading spaces by Herzog & de Meuron.

Thermory Design Awards 2026 recognises striking examples of architecture and design using thermowood

A contemporary take on Ukrainian vernacular buildings and a preschool in Estonia are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified wood.

Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.

Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals.

The treatment enhances the material’s dimensional stability and reduces moisture uptake compared with untreated wood, according to Thermory.

The winner of the interior category is a trio of Ukrainian guesthouses collectively named Under the Reed Roof, designed by Kyiv-based studio YOD Group.

Each guesthouse comprises a glass-walled volume at the base, topped by a tapered thatched roof with exaggerated proportions.

While the exterior of these roofs is made with traditional reeds, the interiors are lined with thermo-ash shingles, arranged to create a tactile effect that is repeated on the front doors.

These highlight the interplay between the interior’s traditional and contemporary design elements, contrasting materials, and the balance between the structure’s openness and enclosure.

“The project stood out to the jury for its exceptionally coherent concept, in which architecture and interior elements come together to form a harmonious whole,” said Thermory.

Winning in the tiny and private house category was Marker Architecture‘s Flooded Gums project, a flood-resilient dwelling built on working farmland.

The building features thermo-ash cladding and thermo-spruce decking, owing to the materials’ robustness and aesthetic merits.

“What particularly impressed the jury was the honesty and clarity of the architecture,” said Thermory of the project.

“Rather than concealing its construction, the project makes its structural logic visible, with every element serving a purpose: the result is a modest yet highly refined building that strikes a compelling balance between aesthetics, functionality and its natural setting,” it added.

Estonia’s Rakke Kindergarten secured the win in the residential, commercial and public building category, thanks to what Thermory describes as local studio Arhitekt Must‘s “cohesive and imaginative design”.

Thermo-spruce cladding, thermo-pine posts and thermo-pine decking all feature in the design, enhancing both its functionality and visual appeal.

The building’s function as an educational environment is made distinctive by the space’s inventive ceiling, which is composed of the short thermo-pine posts, arranged in a way that creates an engaging optical illusion.

“This unexpected architectural gesture elevates a functional space into something distinctive, demonstrating how thoughtful detailing can shape the character and experience of an entire building,” said Thermory.

Finally, the winner of the wellness and spa category is a sauna within the Estonian Embassy in Berlin, designed by interior studio AERIS.

The interiors feature statement walls covered in custom-made oak shingles, which, being circular and slightly overlapping, resemble fish scales.

These are joined by thermo-alder benches and walls, creating a cohesive scheme of timber details that integrate neatly with the lighting design.

“The harmonious interplay of materials, surfaces and light imbues the space with a contemporary edge while retaining the intimacy and warmth of a traditional sauna,” said Thermory.

“Although vastly different in character and purpose, the winning projects share a creative and unconventional approach to design,” it added.

“Each places wood at the heart of its architectural expression, combining imaginative thinking with meticulous attention to detail.”

“Scandinavian design never shouts, but when you come closer, you are rewarded,” says Sara Erichsen Susnjar, senior color and material design manager at Volvo Cars. Detail by detail, the automaker’s new all-electric EX60 bears this out. Its seats carry a pattern drawn from two seas converging off the coast of Skagen, Denmark; its base carpet borrows its hue from foraged finds from the woods outside the company’s studio in Sweden; and an interior lighting option fills the cabin with the silhouettes of leaves.

Erichsen Susnjar, who has spent 20 years at Volvo Cars, oversaw color and materials for both the EX60 and the EX60 Cross Country. Under her direction, the team looked to the natural world for the car’s colors, patterns, and textures, often starting with what turned up on a walk.

Forest Finds

Gathering began close to home, on outings that were already part of the team’s routine. “We are very fortunate to have the forest just outside our design studio, so it naturally becomes part of our everyday life, whether we go there for lunch, a coffee break, or simply to clear our minds,” Erichsen Susnjar says.

Over time, the team began bringing small pieces of the landscape back inside: mushrooms, twigs, stones, moss, and herbs. Each was studied for its pattern, color, and texture, then cast or digitized, and the findings became prompts for new ideas. Traces of the work appear in subtle patterns on the seatbacks and door panels, as well as in the shade of the base carpet. As Erichsen Susnjar puts it, “In that sense, a little piece of the forest has found its way into the car.”

Material Choices

Inside the cabin, material options include tailored wool-blend upholstery and ash wood decor, which sit alongside a 15-inch curved OLED display with Google built-in. “I think bringing natural materials into such a technical and precise environment creates a beautiful contrast,” Erichsen Susnjar explains. “They bring warmth, character and, in a way, a soul to the car. Because natural materials have their own variations and imperfections, they can never be exactly replicated, which means every interior becomes slightly unique.”

Erichsen Susnjar places the cabin’s finer details, including its piping, within a longer regional tradition. “Scandinavian design is very much about those subtle touches,” she says. “They don’t demand your attention, but you discover them over time.”

The EX60 offers six lighting colors, along with Forest Leaves Projection, which brings a canopy of foliage into the interior. The idea came from one of the specialist designers at Volvo Cars, and the team expanded on it to explore how the cabin might feel immersed in woodland.

Outside the cabin, the EX60’s exterior paint colors, among them Forest Lake and Heather Bronze, were developed as a palette that balances light and dark, warm and cool, and complements the colors chosen for the interior. Heather Bronze takes its cue from metals weathered over time and the warm cast of heather fields in autumn.

Crossing Waves

The EX60’s signature motif began when members of the team visited Skagen, where the Skagerrak and Kattegat seas meet, and observed the patterns created by their intersecting waves. Early sketches were refined into a pattern that now appears across the car. It is perforated into the ventilated Nordico upholstery and applied to the subwoofer mesh, the decor panels of the Core version, the rubber floor mats, and the knitted, ventilated seats of the EX60 Cross Country.

Beyond its connection to the Danish coastline, the crossing-wave form also proved useful in production. “There is another layer in this story, and that’s how a pattern like crossing waves was perfect for optimizing the cutting of the materials and minimizing waste,” Erichsen Susnjar says. “And because of that, none of the seats look the same.”

Why it is here: rich vocabulary, profound insights, and clear structure

Silence and Love

Music is the hand of silence cupped to hold the feeling of being alive, lifted to the lips and tasted.

What differentiates music from noise is the touch of silence — the deliberate interstices between the tones, the still points in the rush of sound.

As in music, so in life: “Listen to the silence inside the illusion of the world,” Jack Kerouac wrote to his first wife turned lifelong friend in reckoning with the meaning of life, “and you will remember the lesson you forgot.”

Silence is the listening presence through which you hear the music of your own life, presence purified to become peace — a peace greater than joy and unburdened by understanding, a peace the other word for which may be love.

There is no piece of music that has scored more of my waking days and my writing hours than “Spiegel im Spiegel” by the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, whose virtuosity with sound springs from his relationship to silence — something he articulates with poetic concision in a series of reflections recently shared by his son:

Silence is always more perfect than music. You must simply learn to hear it. Silence is utterly full.

[…]

When we speak of silence, we must keep in mind that it has two wings: Silence can be both outside of us and within us.

The silence of our soul, over which even external noise has no power, is actually more crucial. But is also much more difficult to achieve.

A generation before him, Kahlil Gibran had captured this difficulty with piercing pointedness. “You talk when you cease to be at peace with your thoughts,” he charged in his timeless meditation on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself. Pärt puts it more gently:

One does not have to speak.

But one must love.

One does not have to compose, one does not have to write a book.

But one must love…

If you do not speak, thinking, and even prayer, is clearer, and there is more space left over for love.

I have always felt that the quality of silence two people can share is one of the great measures of love — something the young poet Babette Deutsch captured beautifully a century ago:

SILENCE

by Babette Deutsch

Silence with you is like the faint delicious

Smile of a child asleep, in dreams unguessed:

Only the hinted wonder of its dreaming,

The soft, slow-breathing miracle of rest.

Silence with you is like a kind departure

From iron clangor and the engulfing crowd

Into a wide and greenly barren meadow,

Under the bloom of some blue-bosomed cloud;

Or like one held upon the sands at evening,

When the drawn tide rolls out, and the mixed light

Of sea and sky enshrouds the far, wind-bellowed

Sails that move darkly on the edge of night.

item.description:

Why it is here: deep philosophical content, well-structured, but less focused on music as a metaphor

How to Touch the Nothingness Behind Everything: Kahlil Gibran on the Seven Selves

A self is a forest. A self is a ship. A self is an illusion, and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is a sum of selves, contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

Kahlil Gibran (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life, takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic The Madman (public library | free ebook).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated the Japanese concept of ma.)

THE SEVEN SELVES

by Kahlil Gibran

In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven

selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper:

First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years,

with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow

by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel.

Second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is

given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter

and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance

his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary

existence.

Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand

of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self

who would rebel against this madman.

Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught

was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is

I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell,

who would protest against serving this madman.

Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self,

the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without

rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is

I, not you, who would rebel.

Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who,

with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images

and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the

solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman.

Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this

man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to

fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined

lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits

in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating

life. Is it you or I, neighbours, who should rebel?

When the seventh self thus spake the other six selves looked with

pity upon him but said nothing more; and as the night grew deeper

one after the other went to sleep enfolded with a new and happy

submission.

But the seventh self remained watching and gazing at nothingness,

which is behind all things.

Couple with Gibran on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself, then revisit Hermann Hesse on discovering the soul beneath the self.
